Whether a mother works outside the home makes no material difference to a child's achievement (r = 0.032), and no difference appeared by socioeconomic status, ethnicity, child's age, family structure, or part-time versus full-time work.

Achievement is more closely linked to the socio-psychological environment and intellectual stimulation of the home than to socioeconomic indicators such as parental occupation and education, with maternal involvement, variety of experience and play materials the factors most consistently correlated with achievement.

The relationship between television viewing and achievement is non-linear rather than uniformly negative: up to roughly two hours a day the association is small and positive, beyond that it turns negative and strengthens up to about 35 to 40 hours a week.

The viewing time that remains harmless declines with age — younger children can watch more without effect, by about age seven the threshold is one hour, and by seventeen it is effectively zero; adverse effects were greater for females and for high-IQ students.

Differences in achievement by viewing time may reflect parental characteristics rather than television itself: parents who allowed unrestricted, unsupervised viewing held fewer expectations and lower educational aspirations for their children.

The displacement hypothesis — that television crowds out reading, sport and time with friends — found no support, and television's positive effects on pro-social behaviour (d = 0.63) outweigh its effects on anti-social behaviour (d = 0.30).

Parental involvement is not one thing: a surveillance approach produces negative effects, involvement in early intervention produces low effects, and parental aspirations, expectations and active engagement in the learning itself produce much higher effects.

Parental supervision in the form of monitoring homework, television time and going out with friends had a negative effect on adolescent students' educational aspirations, while parental aspirations were the most important parental influence on achievement.

Parental participation (d = 0.56) and supportive parenting (0.43) relate far more strongly to achievement than homework supervision (0.19), participating in school activities (0.14), communicating with the school (0.14), monitoring progress (0.12), providing home structure (0.00) or a controlling and disciplining style (-0.09).
The family behaviours that relate negatively to achievement are external rewards, homework surveillance, negative control, and restrictions imposed for unsatisfactory grades.

The higher the parents' hopes and expectations for their child's educational attainment, the higher the student's own expectations and ultimately their achievement, and this chain is assisted by parent-student communication and by the student having control over their own studies.
Parental involvement has its largest effect between kindergarten and grade 3 (d = 0.41), declines through grades 3 to 5 (0.36) and reaches roughly zero by secondary school (-0.05).

Among forms of parental involvement, tutoring (d = 0.49) and home visits with teacher interaction (0.48) worked best and parent training worked worst (0.15), with effects far larger in reading (0.40) than mathematics (0.18).

Parental expectations dominate all other parental behaviours as a predictor of achievement — d = 0.58 against 0.21 for parental involvement at the school, and d = 0.88 for secondary students against 0.32 for checking homework, 0.14 for attending school functions and effectively zero for household rules.

Parents teaching their children specific literacy skills was twice as effective (d = 1.15) as listening to the child read (0.51), which in turn was far more effective than reading to the child (0.18); the pattern held from kindergarten to grade 3, for children with and without reading difficulties, and across socioeconomic groups.

Home visiting produced modest cognitive gains generally (d = 0.18) but much larger social-behavioural gains for learning-disabled students (d = 1.01), driven by improvements in parenting (1.06) and parent social functioning (1.52).

Across all home variables, parental aspirations and expectations have the strongest relationship with achievement (d = 0.80), communication about school work is moderate (0.38), and home supervision such as television rules and study surroundings is weakest (0.18).

Schools should partner with parents to make parental expectations appropriately high and challenging and then work with home and child to realize or surpass them, because alienation of home from school erodes the expectations parents start with.

In one low-socioeconomic community 98 per cent of parents rated education as very or extremely important when their children started school and two-thirds expected them to gain diplomas or degrees, yet by the end of elementary school those aspirations had collapsed to wanting the child to get a job.

It is not the structure of the family — single or two parents, resident or non-resident father, divorce, adoption, only child — but the beliefs and expectations of the adults in the home that contribute most to achievement.

Multi-level modelling shows a substantial proportion of achievement variance lies within schools rather than between them, so the teachers students are assigned to may matter more than the schools they attend.

Between zero and 20 per cent of achievement variance is attributable to school-level variables against 16 to 60 per cent to differences between teachers or classes, with the split varying by country policy; adjusted for students' initial differences, schools account for about eight per cent.

Pressure and support for change should be directed at particular teachers within schools rather than at whole schools, since effective schools are effective to the extent that they have effective teachers.

The within-school dominance reverses in less resourced nations and in countries with highly stratified school types, where most variability is between schools; teacher variance is also lower for elementary reading, where family and community input is strong, than for mathematics and other areas less linked to everyday home experience.
exception: Does not hold in less resourced nations, in highly stratified school systems, or for elementary reading.

statement: Among school-level influences, acceleration (d = 0.88) and classroom behavioural interventions (0.80) rank highest, followed by classroom cohesion and peer influences (0.53), classroom management (0.52) and small-group learning (0.49), while class size (0.21), charter schools (0.20), ability grouping (0.12), open versus traditional classrooms (0.01), retention (-0.16) and student mobility (-0.34) sit at or below the bottom; the school category averages d = 0.23.

The relationship between educational expenditure and achievement is minimal, with the most positive relationship running through instructional costs such as teacher salaries and supplies; across 23 countries the correlation between high-school spending per pupil and mathematics scores was r = 0.06.

It is not the amount of money spent on schooling but how it is spent that matters, and money is too often added to the system with little attention to the efficiency or effectiveness of the resulting outcomes.

One rebuttal analysis found systematic positive relations between resource inputs and outcomes — a $500 rise in per-pupil expenditure gave d = 0.15, with teacher education 0.22, teacher experience 0.18, teacher salary 0.16 and teacher-student ratio 0.04 — but there is little evidence to justify calling these increases substantial.

The apparently small effect of school finance is partly an artefact: most studies come from well-resourced countries where variance between schools is small, most school money is tied up in fixed costs rather than discretionary spending, and composition effects that matter sit within rather than between schools while most analysis is between schools.

The productive question is not whether money makes a difference but how it makes a difference above and beyond the fixed costs of running a school; financial incentives currently attach to school rather than teacher differences, so few incentives exist for a teacher to maximise achievement.

The charter-school achievement advantage of d = 0.20 dropped to zero once lower-quality studies were excluded, and only eight of the 38 states with charter laws had usable independent evaluations, so the hype and promise far exceed the measured effect.

African American and Hispanic students attending religious schools showed a d = 0.25 advantage over public-school peers, consistent across reading and mathematics and slightly higher for school-related behaviour (0.32), and the difference could not be attributed to socioeconomic variables.

Summer school produces small gains (about d = 0.23) that are larger for middle-class than for disadvantaged students and larger for high than for low achievers, so a programme usually justified by helping marginal students tends to widen rather than close the gap.

Summer-school design features made essentially no difference to the outcome — purpose (remediation, enrichment, bridging, grade promotion), curriculum linkage, monitoring, teacher training, use of the school's own teachers, provision of food, class size above or below 25, and total hours of instruction all produced similar small effects.
exception: One analysis did find higher effects where the programme was tailored to student needs, parents were involved, and the subject was mathematics rather than reading.

statement: Meta-analyses of desegregation vary widely in effect size mainly according to how articles were selected, and the better-designed quasi-experiments yield considerably smaller effects (falling from about d = 0.45 to d = 0.20 once selection problems are removed).

Where desegregation showed achievement effects they were concentrated in the earliest primary grades (d = 0.44 against about 0.08 overall in one analysis) and in reading rather than mathematics, and studies of more than one year showed effects while shorter ones did not.
Factors other than classroom composition matter more to achievement, so desegregation may be better assessed by the opportunities and diversity it provides than by its achievement effects.

Whether a college student lives in a residence hall, at home, in a fraternity house or off campus makes no difference to achievement (d = 0.05), which should lead residential institutions to question the educational value they add.

School size relates to achievement curvilinearly with an optimum around 600 to 900 students: both much smaller and much larger schools reduce effectiveness, and consolidating very small high schools matters more than consolidating large ones.
The optimal school size shifts with cohort composition: the more affluent the student body the larger the optimum, and the higher the proportion of minority students the smaller the optimum.
condition: Applies when choosing or consolidating school size for a given student population.

statement: Beyond a certain organizational size total output rises but the ratio of output to input stays flat, especially in organizations that depend on human effort such as schools, because coordination costs rise with no matching return.

Mid-sized high schools show more teacher collaboration and team teaching, more teacher input into decisions affecting their work, better personal interaction, more student leadership opportunity, and typically a strong core curriculum for all students with less use of electives to stream and dilute it.

Achievement lost over the summer vacation is small (d = -0.09, slightly larger in mathematics at -0.14 than reading at -0.05) and grows with grade level, but middle-class students gained on reading recognition over the summer (0.13) while lower-class students lost (-0.14).
If teachers were more attuned to the proficiencies students actually bring into the classroom, the first month of the school year could recapture summer losses quickly.

Student mobility between schools carries the most negative effect of any school influence (d = -0.34), affecting reading and mathematics alike, at a time when about 40 per cent of New Zealand students change school each year and 20 per cent of United States students change residence.
It is any change of school that produces the mobility penalty: the effect is unrelated to the total number of moves, to socioeconomic status, or to ethnicity.

The mobility penalty runs through peer effects and disrupted friendship patterns, particularly friendships that support learning; the key success factor at any school transition is whether the child makes a friend in the first month, so schools must actively manage newcomer friendships.

Out-of-school and after-school tutoring programmes produce negligible overall gains (d = 0.09) compared with what effective teachers achieve in regular classrooms, though shorter programmes and one-on-one tutoring (d = 0.50 in reading) do better than long or group formats.

Instructional leadership — focused on a learning climate free of disruption, clear teaching objectives, and high expectations for teachers and students — outperforms transformational leadership on student outcomes (d = 0.55 against 0.09 in one analysis).

The instructional-leadership dimensions with the largest effects on student outcomes are promoting and participating in teacher learning and development (d = 0.91), planning, coordinating and evaluating teaching and curriculum through classroom visits and feedback to teachers (0.74), strategic resourcing aligned to teaching priorities (0.60), establishing goals and expectations (0.54), and protecting teaching time in an orderly, supportive environment (0.49).

The more leaders focus their influence, their own learning and their relationships with teachers on the core business of teaching and learning, the greater their influence on student outcomes; transformational leadership's generic focus on leader-follower relations may explain its weaker student effect.

School leaders have most effect when they promote challenging goals and then establish safe environments in which teachers can critique, question and support one another in reaching those goals together.

Transformational leadership does have a very strong relationship with teacher job satisfaction (r = 0.71) and is what teachers prefer, so leadership style must be evaluated separately for teacher satisfaction and for student achievement.
Principal effects on achievement are much larger at elementary level (d = 0.76) than at middle (0.36) or high school (0.44).

The leadership behaviours that most influence student outcomes are creating a conversation that challenges the school's achievement status quo, supplying current and diverse ways to address it, involving teachers in designing and implementing improvement strategies, setting challenging achievement goals, and monitoring the use of feedback about student progress and teaching effectiveness.

Principal attributes correlating most with achievement are awareness of the school goals needing attention (r = 0.66), keeping teachers intellectually stimulated about current theory and practice (0.64), willingness to challenge the status quo (0.60), monitoring the effect of school practices on learning (0.56), operating from strong beliefs about schooling (0.50) and current knowledge of curriculum, instruction and assessment (0.48).

The principal attributes least related to effectiveness are recognising and rewarding individual accomplishments (r = 0.30), visibility and quality contact with teachers and students (0.32), awareness of teachers' personal circumstances (0.38) and adapting leadership style to the situation (0.44).

In principal assessment centres the strongest correlates of enhanced student outcomes were organizational ability and leadership (r = 0.25) and written communication skill (0.24), while transformational criteria such as sensitivity, range of interests and personal motivation had almost no effect on job performance; neither gender nor ethnicity affected assessment-centre scores on any dimension.

Among organizational development interventions, goal setting (d = 0.22) and team building (0.30) were the more successful and technostructural interventions such as job redesign and job enrichment the least.

Organic management — shifting from hierarchy to a network of control with line employees in decision making and collegiality as coordination — shows almost no evidence of positive effects on student achievement.

Reducing class size from about 25 to 15 produces an effect of roughly d = 0.10 to 0.20 (average d = 0.13), and the estimates vary remarkably little across meta-analyses, longitudinal and cross-cohort designs, countries and grade levels.
The gain from reducing class size is small relative to other available interventions and does not justify the cost of reducing the number of children per classroom.
Reducing class size appears to affect teacher and student work-related conditions more than learning, and those improved conditions may or may not translate into effects on student learning.

The main reason class-size reduction yields so little is that teachers of smaller classes carry on with the teaching methods they used in larger classes and so never exploit the opportunity the smaller class creates.

What counts as excellent teaching changes with class size — from transmitting content to self-regulated learners at 80 or more, through script-following and uniform pacing at 30 to 80, to grouping, peer interaction and tailored curriculum at 20 to 30 — so moving between size bands demands a re-conceptualization of teaching excellence rather than a tweak of method.

The claim that other powerful influences would work better in smaller classes is not borne out: where class sizes were smaller and those influences were implemented, student outcomes still did not differ greatly.

Retraining teachers to work differently with smaller classes might let the optimal strategies take effect, but merely putting fewer students in front of the same teaching changes little in either practice or outcomes.

The class-size evidence summarizes past reductions rather than predicting what a differently implemented reduction could achieve, and the positive sign of the average effect still means that increasing class size is poor policy.

Open versus traditional classroom organization makes essentially no difference to learning outcomes (d = 0.01), with traditional settings marginally ahead on achievement tests and open settings marginally ahead on creativity and attitude in some analyses.
Open classroom architecture is no guarantee that the principles of open teaching are actually present, so a structural label cannot be read as evidence of the practice it names.

The open-education features that distinguished effective from ineffective programmes on non-achievement outcomes were emphasis on the child's role in learning, diagnostic evaluation, manipulative materials and individualized instruction; multi-age grouping, open space and team teaching distinguished nothing.
Programmes that were very effective for non-achievement outcomes produced smaller than average effects on academic achievement, so gains on attitude and self-concept can come at a cost in attainment.

Ability grouping and tracking have minimal effects on learning outcomes across more than 300 studies (average d = 0.11, reading 0.00, mathematics 0.02, self-concept near zero) and no track benefits: high-tracked d = 0.14, middle-tracked -0.03, low-tracked 0.09.

Tracking combines minimal achievement effects with profound negative equity effects, limiting the schooling opportunities, achievements and life chances of students outside the highest tracks, who meet fewer intellectual challenges, less engaging classrooms and fewer well-trained teachers.
Ability grouping shapes friendship networks around track membership, polarizing attitudes so that high-track students grow more enthusiastic and low-track students more alienated.

Qualitative study of low-track classes found deadening, non-educational environments used as holding tanks for students with severe behaviour problems, teaching reduced to dull repetitious seatwork, and tacit agreements between teachers and students not to push each other.

Track placement tracks social advantage as much as attainment: minority students were seven times more likely to be identified as low- than high-ability, Asian students were assigned to advanced courses more often than Hispanic students with equivalent test scores, and average-ability students from advantaged families reached higher tracks through effective parental management.

Schools with more minority and lower-socioeconomic students are less likely to offer sufficient higher-level courses, and the higher-track classes they do offer are often less rigorous than those in schools with more advantaged intakes.

Detracking is concentrated in low-achieving, poor and urban schools while wealthy, high-achieving suburban schools are embracing tracking, which cuts against the account of elites imposing a counterproductive policy on others.

The tracking conundrum resolves to teaching quality rather than structure: the near-zero measured effect sits alongside sharply different teaching in low and high tracks, and if low-track classrooms were stimulating, challenging and well taught there might be gains — but they are not, so the key issues are the quality of teaching and the nature of student interaction, not the compositional structure of classes.

Multi-grade and multi-age classes are neither better nor worse than single-grade classes: achievement effects are essentially zero (d = 0.00 and -0.03) with small positive effects on attitude to school, self-concept and personal adjustment (0.10 and 0.15).

Teachers rarely exploit the multi-grade arrangement to promote peer learning: they teach distinct curricula, maintain grade levels and deliver separate lessons per grade group, and students in multi-grade independent work were less productive and seldom worked cooperatively or helped one another.

One critique argues the multi-grade null result masks a small negative effect of about -0.10 because selection bias puts better students and teachers into those classes; a reanalysis found near-zero cognitive effects overall, small positives in grades 1 to 3 (0.06) turning negative by grades 6 to 7 (-0.08), possible harm in science (-0.19) and mathematics (-0.25), but no support for the selection explanation.

A deeply embedded grammar of teaching persists regardless of structural change to classes, so teachers teach in much the same way whatever the age distribution or organization of the class — which is why such structural reforms return close-to-zero findings.

Within-class grouping — semi-permanent ability groups formed inside one class — gives a modest advantage over no grouping (d = 0.17 to 0.25) and benefits low-, medium- and high-ability students alike.
The benefit of within-class grouping depends on class size: it is largest in classes above 35 students (d = 0.35), moderate below 26 (0.22) and close to nothing in classes of 26 to 35 (0.06).
condition: The advantage holds most strongly in large classes.

statement: Small-group instruction gains more against traditional whole-class teaching (d = 0.24) than against individualized mastery learning (0.15), and small groups working cooperatively outperform other small groups (0.28 against 0.15).

Small-group learning, where a task is assigned to a group who must complete it, outperformed individual learning on achievement, group task performance and affective outcomes, with gains significantly enhanced when students had prior group-work experience or instruction, when specific cooperative learning strategies were used, and when the group was small.
condition: Enhanced where students have group-work experience or instruction, cooperative learning strategies are used, and group size is small.

statement: The only meta-analyses of small-group learning were conducted at tertiary level, which limits how far its roughly d = 0.5 effect on achievement, attitude and persistence can be generalized to schools.

Simply placing students into small or more homogeneous groups is not enough: for grouping to be maximally effective the instructional materials and the teaching must be varied and made appropriately challenging for each group's level.

Least restrictive environment does not mean simply placing a student with disabilities in a regular class; it refers to modification of content, materials, classroom management, instructional techniques and strategies.

Mainstreaming shows small positive advantages over special classes for comparable students (about d = 0.08 to 0.12, achievement 0.15, social and personality 0.11), with larger effects for students classified as mentally retarded (0.47) than learning disabled (0.13).

There is very little compelling evidence of any compositional effect from single-sex versus mixed-sex classes; a study that randomized students and teachers found no gains for girls in girls-only or boys in boys-only mathematics classes, and brighter students benefited more from mixed-sex classes.

Comparisons of single-sex and coeducational classes are confounded by non-equivalent groups, because single-sex classes tend to be selective in both students and teachers, so any difference may reflect selection rather than class composition.
The quality of teaching and teacher expectations produce far more powerful effects than whether a class is single-sex or mixed.
exception: Most of this research was conducted with high school students; there is minimal research at elementary level.

statement: Grade retention is among the very few practices in education where almost no study shows a positive effect: the most recent synthesis of 169 achievement effects gave d = -0.39, with reading -0.54, mathematics -0.49, socio-emotional outcomes -0.22 and attendance -0.65.

The damage from retention compounds over time: retained students were 0.45 standard deviations behind their promoted comparison group after one year and 0.83 standard deviations behind four or more years later, even though the promoted group was being tested on more advanced material.
Being retained one year almost doubles a student's likelihood of dropping out and failing twice almost guarantees it, making retention the second greatest predictor of school drop-out.

Retention's harm is partly caused by schools not providing any special intervention for the retained student, so the child simply repeats a programme that already failed them, and partly by peer-group effects of being forced to work with students of a different age.

Retention carries severe equity effects: given two students of the same achievement, the student of colour is about four times more likely to be retained and the white student promoted, and those held back are more likely to be poor and male.

The threat of non-promotion is not a motivating force for students, and retention is a poor use of the education dollar because it adds an extra year of schooling cost without benefit for the vast majority of retained children.
For gifted students, acceleration is by far the most effective provision (d = 0.84) against enrichment (0.39) and ability grouping (0.30), yet it is the least implemented of the three.

Gifted programmes must be distinguished from high-ability tracks: tracks give a faster pace and harder tasks within the same curriculum, while gifted programmes often use different curricula, and it is specific curricula aimed at challenging students at the appropriate level that make engagement and learning more likely.

Accelerated students outperformed non-accelerated students of equivalent age and intelligence by nearly a full grade level (d = 0.88), performed as well as the brighter students in the grades they moved into, and held higher educational ambitions without any drop in school participation.

The social objection to acceleration is not supported: gifted students in accelerated programmes showed slightly positive social effects (d = 0.13) with negative effects for those not accelerated, so the question to ask is what social harm follows from failing to accelerate a gifted student.

No study has shown enrichment to produce superior results to acceleration; at best enrichment may only defer boredom, and resistance to acceleration usually rests on preconceived claims about social and emotional acceptability or on timetabling barriers.

Enrichment worked far better in mathematics (d = 1.10) and science (1.23) than reading (0.59) or social studies (0.23), and programmes where students mastered more mature ideas outperformed broader sweeps through the regular curriculum.
Teacher experience with gifted students transformed enrichment outcomes: experienced teachers achieved d = 0.88 while those with no or limited experience achieved d = -0.06.

Well-managed classrooms raise achievement (d = 0.52) and engagement (0.62), and the teacher attributes that matter most are 'with-it-ness' (d = 1.42) — the ability to spot and act quickly on a potential behaviour problem — an appropriate mental set (1.29) and emotional objectivity (0.71).

Beyond teacher awareness, the strongest classroom-management methods are disciplinary interventions signalling whether behaviour is appropriate (d = 1.00), group contingency strategies (0.98), tangible recognition (0.82) and direct concrete consequences for misbehaviour (0.57).

Teacher-student relationships powerfully moderate classroom management (d = 0.87), combining high dominance — clarity of purpose and strong guidance — with high cooperation, meaning concern for others' needs and opinions and a desire to work as part of a team.
Rules and procedures raise achievement (d = 0.76) when expectations are stated, well articulated and negotiated with students.
condition: Effective where the rules and procedures are negotiated with students rather than imposed.

statement: Classroom cohesion — the sense that teachers and students are all working towards positive learning gains — is the key factor in a positive classroom climate, alongside goal directedness, positive interpersonal relations and social support; friction, cliquishness, apathy and disorganization work against learning.
The cohesion-performance relationship is stable, positive, stronger in smaller classroom groups, and attributable to commitment to the task rather than to interpersonal attraction or group pride.
Greater classroom cohesiveness makes co-peer learning, tolerance and welcoming of error, increased feedback, and discussion of goals and success criteria more likely.

Reducing disruptive behaviour must be a core competency of any successful teacher, and the aim is not to remove the disruptive student — the same student is often less disruptive in a different class — but to ensure no student needlessly disrupts their own or others' learning.

Behavioural interventions against disruption clearly outperform non-behavioural ones (d = 0.76 against 0.35), and the most successful specific approaches are social or token reinforcement (1.38), behavioural consultation (1.09), cooperation (1.05) and cognitive behaviour modification (1.0), while social skills training is the least successful (0.44).
Programmes targeting academic outcomes had the greatest effect on disruptive students, ahead of those targeting classroom behaviour or social interactions.

Studies using teacher rating scales were less likely than those using direct behavioural observation to show reductions in disruptive classroom behaviour, so the measurement method changes the apparent success of an intervention.

Peers influence learning by helping, tutoring, providing friendship, giving feedback and making school somewhere students want to come, and by supplying social comparison, emotional support, social facilitation, cognitive restructuring and rehearsal — yet peers are rarely involved in the teaching and learning process.

Friendships raise achievement by carrying caring, support and help and easing conflict resolution, and their influence is strongest from early adolescence, when the quality of a friendship magnifies its effect and the reputations it confers can help or harm academic achievement.

Performance-oriented students, focused on proving achievement relative to others, may take on less challenging tasks in order to demonstrate competence, whereas mastery-oriented students who value learning in itself attend to their own academic development.

Low classroom peer acceptance links consistently to student disengagement and lower achievement, because exclusion restricts access to the social and instrumental resources carried in class peer activities.

School uniform policies had no effect on academic achievement in elementary school and a significant negative effect at high school level, no effect on attendance, self-esteem, locus of control, coping skills, drug use or behaviour incidents, and did not improve — and at middle school worsened — perceptions of school safety; dress codes show the same absence of effect.

A striking feature of school-effects research is how many issues generate heat proportional to an obviously effective policy while the achievement evidence sits at or below zero — class size, tracking, retention, summer schools, school uniforms — so the visible discourse of schooling is dominated by cosmetic reform.

Many structural debates concern teachers' working conditions, and while working conditions are worth pursuing in their own right, focusing on them displaces debate about the matters that actually affect student achievement.

The powerful school-level moves are classroom climate, peer influences, absence of disruptive students, adapting curricula to be appropriately challenging through acceleration or differentiated gifted provision, and principals who act as instructional leaders; mainstreaming, ability grouping, class size, open classrooms, multi-grade classes and summer courses sit near zero, and retention and student mobility are negative.

Nearly all teachers are effective in the trivial sense of producing an effect above zero, so what matters is teachers' variability in effect and impact, and how many can reach the zone of desired effects above d = 0.40.

Students typically name only two or three of the 40 to 60 teachers they encounter as having made a real difference — around four to six per cent — and the ones they name turned them on to the love and challenge of the subject.

Asked about their best teachers, students name those who built relationships with them, who gave them different and better strategies for learning the subject, and who showed a willingness to explain material and help with their work.

Between seven and 21 per cent of the variance in achievement gains is associated with variation in teacher effectiveness (average d = 0.32), meaning a one-standard-deviation rise in teacher effectiveness raises achievement gains by about a third of a standard deviation.

Teacher effects are much larger in low-socioeconomic schools, so it matters more which teacher a child is assigned to in a low-socioeconomic school than in a high-socioeconomic one; teacher effectiveness also varies more for mathematics (11 per cent) than reading (7 per cent).
Neither teacher experience nor teacher education explained much of the variance in teacher effects — never more than five per cent.

Among teacher-side influences, teacher clarity (d = 0.75) and teacher-student relationships (0.72) rank highest, followed by professional development (0.62), not labeling students (0.61), quality of teaching (0.44) and expectations (0.43), while teacher training (0.11) and teacher subject-matter knowledge (0.09) sit near the bottom; microteaching is the outlier at 0.88.

Student teachers already 'know' a great deal about teaching from years of watching it, and will interpret any new skill or theory through what they already believe, so the central task of teacher learning is to change those conceptions rather than to add skills.

Student teachers must be moved from seeing classrooms through their own eyes as students to seeing learning through the eyes of the students in front of them, and must be persuaded that subjects are more than the facts they learned, that teaching is more than personal craft and common sense, and that a strong desire to control student behaviour can be inconsistent with many conceptual approaches to teaching.

The effect of teacher education on subsequent student outcomes is negligible (about d = 0.10), and fully certified teachers hold only a slight advantage over probationary or emergency-licensed ones (about d = 0.12), though teachers trained in the field they teach do markedly better (d = 0.38).

The gain of certified over emergency-licensed teachers rises to d = 0.39 only when the certified group also has several years of teaching experience, which probably reflects accumulated pedagogical content knowledge rather than subject-matter knowledge itself.

Accreditation of teacher education should rest on evidence that graduates meet articulated graduating standards and go on to affect their own students, not on whether the college has the right staff and enough time on task.

Microteaching and laboratory experience — mini-lessons to a small group, videotaped, followed by analysis and debriefing — produce moderate to strongly positive effects on teacher knowledge and instructional behaviour (d = 0.70 to 0.88) that do not significantly decay over time, yet these methods are far less used today.

Within teacher training, demonstration works best for knowledge (d = 1.65) and attitude (0.48) while theory works best for skills (0.97), so theory, demonstration, practice, feedback and coaching should all be included and distributed across many sessions rather than condensed.
Most teacher programmes train low-level skills that reinforce what the trainee already does, with too little exposure to new conceptions of teaching and new ways of teaching.

Beginning teachers' conceptions of teaching emphasise interpersonal aspects and minimize the academic goals of schooling, treating teaching largely as telling, which is at odds with a model built on challenging learning intentions, success criteria, monitoring one's own effectiveness and optimizing feedback.

Exemplary teacher education programmes share seven features: coherence around a clear vision of good teaching, well-defined standards of practice guiding coursework and clinical work, curriculum grounded in development, learning, social context and subject pedagogy, extended clinical experience interwoven with coursework, explicit strategies for confronting trainees' deep-seated beliefs, shared knowledge and beliefs among all who teach them, and assessment through performance demonstrations and portfolios.

Teacher subject-matter knowledge relates only weakly to student outcomes (d = 0.09 to 0.12, similar at elementary and high school), despite the plausibility of the claim that a teacher must know a subject to teach it; it likely matters up to a basic level of competence and much less thereafter.
condition: Subject-matter knowledge probably does influence effectiveness up to some level of basic competence.

statement: Teachers who score well on verbal ability tests do better in the classroom, and this is close to the most consistent finding across studies of teacher characteristics — but verbal ability may be a correlate of unmeasured attributes such as flexibility, empathy and content knowledge, and correlates must not be read as causes.
Knowledge, empathy and verbal ability are all needed together and are greater than the sum of the parts: if one is missing, effectiveness drops by more than a third.
About a fifth of teachers were not certified in the subject area they taught, with the shortfall far worse in some sciences, which matters because teaching in field carries a measurable advantage.

Pre-service programmes that include interpersonal skills training raise new teachers' positive attitudes and self-concepts (d = 0.30), but those gains decline once teachers begin work, particularly in inner-city schools where they were less well prepared.
Student ratings of teaching quality relate to learning outcomes, but the feedback those ratings give teachers rarely translates into improved teaching or more effective courses.
All meta-analytic evidence relating teaching quality to learning derives from student ratings collected in college and university settings, so its transfer to school settings is an extrapolation.
Quality teaching as students rate it consists of challenging students, holding high expectations, encouraging engagement with the subject, and valuing both surface and deep aspects of the subject.
The dismissal of student ratings as popularity contests is not supported: the majority of studies find them reliable, trustworthy and valid.

Instructor expressiveness moves student ratings substantially but affects achievement only slightly, while lecture content moves achievement substantially but ratings only slightly — so a rating instrument must be read as measuring partly presentation, not solely learning.

Feedback from student ratings makes a medium contribution to improving college teaching (d = 0.38), and the effect is amplified when the feedback is extended through consultation rather than merely delivered.
condition: when the rating feedback is accompanied by consultation

statement: Elementary and high schools should collect student evaluations of teaching rather than rely on the belief that quality is high or that students are too immature to judge, because students sit in the classes and know whether the teacher sees learning through their eyes.

The decisive test of teacher excellence is how students judge it, not how the teacher or colleagues judge it, because students alone can report the quality of the relationship and whether learning is visible to them.

Studies of National Board certification give conflicting accounts of its impact on student achievement, with large-scale growth comparisons reporting effects near zero (d = 0.04 to 0.05) and others reporting small to moderate gains (d = 0.09 to 0.43 by subject).

The strongest discriminator between board-certified and non-certified teachers is setting appropriately challenging goals — systematically and consistently challenging students to think through demanding, engaging assignments (d = 1.37).

Accomplished teachers are further distinguished by testing hypotheses about the effects of their own teaching (d = 1.09) and by holding a deeper understanding of that teaching and its effects on student learning (d = 1.02).

Accomplished teachers shift the depth of student work rather than test scores: about 74 percent of their students' work samples showed deep (relational or extended abstract) understanding against 29 percent for non-certified teachers, while the writing achievement difference was slight (d = 0.13).

A teacher-quality effect can be invisible on a state test if that test targets surface features of the curriculum while the teaching advantage lies in deeper understanding — so the outcome measure must match the outcome claimed.

The least effective teachers produced average student gains of roughly 14 percentile points a year against 52 for the most effective, so teacher effectiveness is a first-order determinant of a year's growth.

The damage from an ineffective teacher is measurable in later years' achievement and shows little compensatory recovery from more effective teachers in subsequent grades, and it applies to all students in that teacher's class rather than a subgroup.

Raising achievement for all students requires reducing the chance that any student is assigned to a relatively ineffective teacher, which makes teacher assignment a policy lever rather than an administrative detail.
Matching teacher and student race makes essentially no difference to achievement (d = 0.02 reading, d = 0.03 mathematics), so ethnic matching is not a defensible achievement intervention.

When students, parents, principals and teachers are asked what drives achievement, every group except teachers names the teacher-student relationship; teachers instead attribute achievement to the child's attitudes, home or school conditions.

Building relationships with students requires teachable skills — listening, empathy, caring and positive regard — together with recognizing in the classroom what the child brings from home, culture and peers, rather than being a fixed disposition.

Person-centered teacher variables correlate 0.34 (d = 0.72) with student achievement and attitude outcomes across 119 studies and 355,325 students, with the strongest links to critical and creative thinking (r = 0.45) and weakest to grades (r = 0.25).
Classes with person-centered teachers show more engagement, more respect for self and others, fewer resistant behaviors, more student-initiated and student-regulated activity, and higher achievement.

To improve teacher-student relationships teachers should demonstrate care for each student's learning as a person and take the student's perspective back to them, so the student gains usable feedback, feels safe to self-assess, and learns to understand others and the content.

Professional development evaluations mostly report changes in teachers rather than impact on students, so a claim that a program works must state which of the four outcome levels — reaction, teacher learning, teacher behavior, student outcomes — it was measured at.
Professional development effects decay across the outcome chain: teacher learning d = 0.90, teacher behavior d = 0.60, teacher reactions d = 0.42, and student learning only d = 0.37.

The professional-development formats most effective on teacher knowledge and behavior are observing actual classroom methods, microteaching, video or audio feedback, and practice; discussion, lectures, games and simulations, guided field trips, coaching, modeling and producing materials are weaker.
Professional development should be spread over an extended period, except where a powerful idea forms the basis of new practice and has high impact on student outcomes on its own.
exception: when a single powerful idea grounds new practice and independently produces high impact on student outcomes

statement: The most critical driver of professional development's effect on student learning is challenging teachers' prevailing discourse and conceptions about learning — especially the assumption that some groups of students cannot or will not learn as well as others — or challenging how they teach a particular curriculum.

Teachers talking to teachers about teaching is necessary but not sufficient for professional development to affect students: it works only when discussions are grounded in artifacts of student learning and when competing ideas are tested rather than merely shared.
condition: when discussion is grounded in artifacts representing student learning and used to test the efficacy of competing ideas

statement: Involving external experts is more strongly related to professional-development success than within-school initiatives, and school leadership support, access to relevant expertise and time to process new information further raise effectiveness.

Funding, release time, and whether participation is voluntary or compulsory are unrelated to professional development's influence on student outcomes, so these levers should not be treated as quality signals.

The useful question about teacher expectations is not whether teachers hold them — they do, and expectations affect achievement — but whether they hold false or misleading expectations that depress learning, and for which students.

The Pygmalion finding that labeling students as likely bloomers raised their achievement has many failed replications and documented methodological problems, so it should be cited as suggestive rather than established.

Interpersonal expectancy effects average d = 0.70 across 345 experiments and are as large in everyday situations as in the laboratory, implying teachers tend to obtain the outcomes they expect regardless of whether the expectation is accurate.

Routine praise or bare correction carries no information beyond right-or-wrong and so has little impact; the content of feedback matters more than its frequency, timing, or positive-versus-negative valence.

Supplying teachers with pertinent academic information reduces the weight they place on irrelevant cues such as attractiveness, and attractiveness bias is markedly reduced though not eliminated when explicit competence evidence is present.
condition: when explicit academic or competence evidence about the student is available to the teacher

statement: The learning-difficulties label itself depresses performance: 73 percent of unlabeled low achievers scored above the average reading score of labeled low achievers (d = 0.61), despite no evidence the labeled students differ qualitatively in learner characteristics.

Students accurately perceive that they are treated differentially according to teacher expectations and can report which teachers favor some children over others, so student report is a usable instrument for detecting expectancy effects.
A teacher who holds low expectations holds them for every student in the class, making low expectation a teacher-level effect rather than a response to particular students.
Teachers should stop over-emphasizing ability and emphasize progress instead, treating a steep learning curve as the right of every student regardless of starting point.
Teachers should seek evidence that surprises them rather than evidence confirming prior expectations, and be prepared to be surprised as the working defence against negative expectation effects.
If expectations are to be held at all they should be challenging, appropriate to the student, and checkable against what is deemed valuable, rather than left implicit.

Most meta-analyses on labeling students do not use achievement as an outcome; they measure how teachers and parents differentiate labeled from regular students, so a labeling study cannot be cited as evidence about achievement.

Cognitive differences between disabled and non-disabled students are area-specific rather than global: they appear in discrimination learning but not in conservation or incidental learning, so a blanket deficit assumption is unwarranted.

Students categorized with mathematics disabilities underperform age-matched peers most on verbal problem solving (d = -0.58), naming speed and verbal word memory (d = -0.70 each), pointing to verbal working memory rather than numerical ability as the locus.

Low achievers and reading-disabled students share a common phonological processing problem and do not differ in automaticity (d = -0.06) or real-word reading (d = 0.02), so the disability label does not identify a distinct reading mechanism.

Because low achievers and reading-disabled students share a phonological processing deficit, phonics training directly raises reading achievement for these students, particularly spelling and word recognition.
condition: for students with low reading achievement or an identified reading disability

statement: Students classified as brain injured differ from those whose difficulties are familial-cultural by only d = 0.10 across 241 effect sizes, with no dimension exceeding d = 0.14, so this diagnostic distinction carries almost no instructional information.
Labels mainly serve to classify students and unlock funding; they rarely change what works best for those students, so a label should not drive the choice of teaching method.
Teacher clarity — organization, explanation, examples, guided practice and assessment of student learning, with clear speech as a prerequisite — relates to achievement at r = 0.35 (d = 0.75).
Teacher-clarity effects are larger when students rather than observers rate the teacher and for college rather than elementary teachers, while class size and subject taught make no difference.
Communicating the intentions of a lesson and what success on those intentions looks like is a load-bearing teacher behaviour, not a presentational nicety.

The teacher's largest contributions are the quality of the teacher and the nature of teacher-student relationships; expectations and professional development are medium, and teacher education programs are low.

Few teachers actively decrease achievement, but low expectations held for a whole class do systematically depress it, so harm operates through expectation rather than through the teacher being harmful in general.

The above-average effect belongs not to teachers as such but to teachers using particular teaching methods, holding high expectations for all students, and having built positive teacher-student relationships.
Roughly as many teachers fall below the d = 0.40 hinge-point as above it, so which teacher a student is assigned each year is a substantial gamble on that year's growth.

Discussion of teacher quality should be reframed from the personal and professional attributes of teachers to the quality of the effects teachers have on learning, making teaching the more critical object of discussion than teachers.
Initial teacher training programs have little impact on how well their graduates influence student achievement, and the quantity and quality of evidence about teacher training is itself poor.

Teacher education would more plausibly succeed if it emphasized learning and teaching strategies, treated teaching as evidence-based (learning from errors as much as successes), built appraisal on trusted observation or videotaped reflection, and equipped beginners with alternative methods for when the current one fails.

Teacher education should reintroduce micro-skills teaching methods, build understanding of how to teach surface, deep and conceptual knowledge distinctly, and show how student assessment feeds back to the teacher on who was not taught well and what needs re-teaching.

A teacher education program should articulate graduating standards and then be evaluated on the appropriateness of those standards and the quality of evidence that all its students meet them, with employers and independent educationalists sitting alongside the program's own academics in that judgment.
Evidence that teacher subject-matter knowledge matters for student outcomes is hard to find, possibly because nearly all teachers clear an acceptable threshold leaving little variance to detect.

The arguments that deep subject knowledge helps a teacher sequence surface-to-deep progressions and give feedback as students struggle are plausible but lack supporting evidence, so they should be flagged as untested rather than asserted.

The productive research question about subject knowledge is the minimum needed to be an accomplished teacher and how to optimize the teaching strategies of those who have more, rather than whether more is better.
Teachers' conceptions of teaching, learning, curricula, assessment and their students are powerful moderators of their success, so those conceptions are a legitimate target of intervention.

Expectation effects depend less on between-student attributes such as gender or race than on whether the expectation is held high or low for all students, making the class-wide expectation level the variable to check.
Half of all material taught in a class is already known by the students, so a teacher who does not check prior proficiency before starting spends much of the year on redundant content.

Teachers should establish student proficiencies before the year begins by reviewing student records and talking with previous teachers, rather than discovering them by trial and error through the early months.

The single greatest obstacle to further student improvement is the absence of a common conception of progress among teachers, so that a student moving between teachers has no guarantee of increasingly challenging tasks or comparable expectations.
A teacher should grow a student from where that student actually is, not from where the teacher believes the student should be at the start of the year.

Teachers routinely misjudge the state of their relationships because they assume relations are positive and look for confirming cues rather than seeing the classroom through students' eyes; showing them survey evidence of student perceptions prompts rapid change in practice.

A teacher must enter the classroom believing their role is that of a change agent — that all students can learn and progress and that achievement is changeable rather than fixed — for the relationship and expectation effects to operate.

A student who has not developed sufficient reading acumen by the middle of elementary school is handicapped across every other curriculum area, because schooling shifts early from learning to read to reading to learn.

Across 50 reading meta-analyses covering over 2,000 studies and about five million students the average effect is d = 0.51, establishing that reading skills and strategies should be actively taught across all years of schooling.

Reading programs must be planned, deliberate, explicit and active in teaching specific skills — decoding, vocabulary, comprehension and specific strategies — because programs without a skills and strategies emphasis have very minimal effects.

Within reading curricula, vocabulary programs (d = 0.67), repeated reading (d = 0.67), phonics instruction (d = 0.60), comprehension programs (d = 0.58) and visual-perception programs (d = 0.55) clear the hinge-point, while whole language (d = 0.06) and sentence combining (d = 0.15) do not.

Across all curricula the average effect is d = 0.45, with creativity programs (0.65), tactile stimulation (0.58), outdoor and adventure programs (0.52) and play programs (0.50) high, and perceptual-motor programs (0.08) and extra-curricular programs (0.17) near zero.

Auditory and visual perceptual skills predict reading about equally (d = 0.33 to 0.47 across sub-skills) and the ability to integrate perceptual stimuli adds nothing beyond the individual skills, so perceptual-integration training has no distinct warrant.

The widely used Frostig visual-perception test and its training program predict reading achievement significantly less well than other visual-motor and visual-spatial measures, and are not useful for identifying, preparing or remediating young readers.

Vocabulary instruction produces a large gain in comprehension of passages containing the taught words (d = 0.97) but only a small gain on global comprehension measures (d = 0.30), so near-transfer must not be reported as general comprehension improvement.
The most effective vocabulary teaching gives both definitional and contextual information, engages students in deeper processing, and provides more than one or two exposures to each target word.

The mnemonic keyword method improves recall of definitions and sentence comprehension but fades very quickly, with delayed post-test effects as low as d = 0.19, so it should not be relied on for durable vocabulary learning.
exception: when the requirement is durable retention rather than immediate recall

statement: Deriving word meaning from context is amenable to instruction, with even relatively short instruction producing positive effects.

Language intervention benefits language-disordered children more than learning- or reading-disabled children, improves syntax most and pragmatic language functioning least, and works better through a modeling approach than through focused stimulation or comprehension methods.
condition: for children with an identified language disorder

statement: Language intervention gains for intellectually handicapped preschool children hold across demographic, pretreatment language level, handicap type and medical history, but are reduced where there is significant neurological impairment.
exception: where significant neurological impairment is present

statement: The structured and sequential design of a language program, rather than its brand, is the key element in its greater effectiveness.

Systematic phonics instruction teaches a planned, sequenced set of letter-sound correspondences — consonants, short and long vowels, digraphs and letter-sound blends — rather than incidental exposure to the alphabetic code.

Phonics instruction produces d = 0.86 on phonological outcomes, d = 0.59 on spelling and d = 0.53 on reading, so its largest effect is on the proximal skill and its reading effect is materially smaller.
Teaching one or two types of phonemic awareness produces larger effects than teaching many, so breadth of phonemic-awareness coverage should be narrowed rather than expanded.

Manipulating phonemes using letters produces greater effects than manipulating them without letters, and synthetic phonics — converting letters to sounds, blending them into words, then analyzing larger sub-parts — outperforms alternatives.
Phonemic awareness effects hold whether delivered by classroom teachers or computer, and whether by tutoring, small group or whole class, so delivery mode is not the constraint.
Phonemic awareness effects are higher for preschool than for higher grade levels and decrease as age increases, making them most powerful during learning to read rather than later.
condition: during the learning-to-read phase, principally preschool and early elementary

statement: The National Reading Panel findings were contested largely because they drew on very few of the available reading studies, though independent meta-analyses reach similar conclusions.
Phonological awareness training should be treated as a causal factor in learning to read (d = 0.73 randomized, d = 0.70 matched), not merely a correlate.

Long-term phonological training effects are smaller than short-term effects, though phonemic training remains discernible after an average of 18.5 months, so short-term gains must not be reported as durable ones.
Phonological awareness training works better in groups than individually, and programs combining phonological with letter training beat phonological training alone.
Phonological training effects are stronger on post-tests of simple decoding than on real-word identification, so the outcome measure inflates or deflates the apparent effect.
The most effective configuration is phonics combined with additional language and literacy activities, with phonics, fluency and comprehension as the core ingredients.
Phonemic awareness instruction benefits low socioeconomic status students as much as middle and high status students, contradicting the claim that it disadvantages poorer children.

The most successful phonemic awareness program targeted word recognition skills and ran for more than 1.5 hours over more than 8 weeks (d = 1.02), so dosage and duration are part of the intervention definition.
condition: when delivered for more than 1.5 hours across more than 8 weeks

statement: Direct instruction methods are the most powerful way to teach phonics skills, and combining direct instruction with taught word-recognition strategies improves reading comprehension for students with learning disabilities.
The greatest predictors of reading comprehension are real-word reading and spelling ability, followed by word attack skills, so these are the diagnostic measures to collect.

Sentence-combining instruction has small and ambiguous effects on reading comprehension and does not warrant a place in the reading instruction toolkit, though it is more effective at elementary than high school level.
The largest source of variance in repeated-reading effects is test format: timed tests show larger effects than untimed because they assess automatic application of word recognition and decoding.

Automaticity in word recognition and decoding develops naturally between second and third grade, but for learning-disabled students it is a separate skill set that must be specifically assessed and taught.
condition: for learning-disabled students, in whom automaticity does not emerge unaided

statement: Repeated reading improves both fluency and comprehension, with near transfer to the practised passage (d = 0.76) larger than far transfer to new passages (d = 0.50), though far transfer remains substantial.

Comprehension-program effects are larger on narrow outcomes than broad ones — vocabulary d = 1.77 against reading comprehension d = 0.70, and word-level units d = 1.28 against whole-text units d = 0.82 — so the unit of analysis drives the headline number.

Comprehension programs focused on processing strategies such as inferential reasoning, summarizing rules and text chunking outperform text-focused (d = 0.77) and task-focused (d = 0.69) programs at d = 1.04, and work about equally for poor and good readers.

Both visually dependent and auditory or language dependent comprehension strategies produce large effects (d = 0.94 and d = 1.18), but only because the teacher explicitly taught those strategies — the materials alone do not carry the effect.
condition: only when the teacher explicitly teaches the strategy rather than supplying the materials

statement: The claim that reading method makes little difference to achievement holds broadly except for sound-symbol blending, where systematic synthesis of separate letter sounds is superior to other methods.
exception: except for sound-symbol blending methods, which are superior

statement: A concept-oriented reading program that pairs comprehension mini-lessons with motivational engagement raises multiple-text comprehension (d = 0.93), fluency (d = 0.73) and self-efficacy (d = 0.49), showing motivation and strategy instruction can be addressed together.

Students learn only about 15 percent of the unknown words they meet during normal reading, so incidental acquisition cannot carry vocabulary growth and the premise behind high-frequency-reading approaches is weak.
Incidental word learning is confounded with reading ability — older and abler students learn more words from reading — so a poor reader will not improve vocabulary simply by being asked to read more.
A low density of unknown words in a text yields more incidental word learning than a high density, so text difficulty must be matched to the learning goal.

The apparent positive result for whole language rests on classifying as whole language studies that in fact taught phonological recoding, word lists, letter-sound naming and decoding; reclassifying three such studies moves that meta-analysis from d = 0.65 to zero and the pooled average to d = 0.06, ranked 129 of 138.

Divergent meta-analytic results for the same intervention can be traced to how primary studies were coded and classified, so a coding audit is required before treating two syntheses as contradictory evidence.

Whole language yields near-zero effects on word recognition (d = 0.17) and comprehension (d = 0.09), and low socioeconomic status children given basal readers consistently outperform those given whole language instruction.
Whole language does improve children's attitudes towards reading even though it is negligible for learning to read, so an attitude gain must not be reported as a reading-skill gain.
Whole language may have value for later reading but not for the process of learning to read; reading strategies need to be deliberately taught, especially to struggling readers.

The effect of exposing children to reading depends on who reads: teachers reading aloud as a teaching tool produce d = 0.63 on oral language and d = 0.41 on reading, while volunteers have little or no effect.
Reading-aloud effects are higher with younger students and small groups because those conditions foster more interaction between reader, child and text.
condition: with younger children and in small groups

statement: Parent-preschooler joint book reading relates to language growth (d = 0.67), emergent literacy (d = 0.58) and reading achievement (d = 0.55) across all socioeconomic groups, with effects diminishing as children become able to read alone.
Reading to children is not sufficient to produce competent readers — instruction is also needed, and exposure or practice in listening to reading does not substitute for it.
There is little good evidence that using unpaid classroom volunteers to help teach reading is effective — almost half those studies showed negative effects.

More reading practice is only minimally associated with reading gains (d = 0.10), slightly larger for grades 1 to 3, second-language, learning-disabled and below-grade students — practice helps marginally but is not enough.

Sustained silent reading has little effect on reading attitude and none above grade 3; for students who struggle or dislike reading it can become another occasion confirming that reading is not enjoyable.

Reading Recovery produces large effects for at-risk readers (d = 0.96 overall; comprehension 0.67, decoding 0.56, oral word reading 0.69), and the effect is highest when it supplements rather than substitutes for classroom teaching.
condition: when delivered as a supplement to, not a replacement for, regular classroom instruction

statement: Well-designed, reliably implemented one-to-one interventions can make a significant contribution for students whose poor reading places them at risk of academic failure.
condition: when the intervention is well designed and reliably implemented

statement: Attending to all five pillars of reading instruction — phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary and comprehension — matters far more than which single pillar a program emphasizes.

The most powerful reading sequence is to attend first to visual and auditory perceptual skills, then combine vocabulary, comprehension and phonics instruction with repeated reading opportunities; the least effective are whole language, sentence combining and relying on incidental vocabulary learning.

A teacher using whole language would need to be at least ten times more effective than a teacher using phonics to reach the same reading outcomes, and a teacher combining vocabulary, phonics and comprehension outperforms either single-method teacher.

Reading research concentrates on the early years, with no meta-analyses and only limited evidence about teaching reading beyond the first years, so recommendations for older readers rest on weaker ground.

Reading achievement plateaus rather than slumps in upper elementary years: more than 80 percent of year 5 students are at or above expectation, close to half fall below by year 8, and about 80 percent are above again by year 11.

Candidate causes of the upper-elementary reading plateau include no common teacher conception of reading progress, curricula that omit reading progressions, and an emphasis on early reading that leaves no perceived need for later programs.

Previously unimportant reading difficulties surface around grade 5 when students first meet informational materials and multiple text types demanding inference, comprehension and low-frequency vocabulary.

Reading growth resumes in high school where teachers demand the higher-level skills of finding information, making connections, inferring and understanding within content-area literacy, suggesting those demands are what upper-elementary teaching lacks.
Teaching strategies for planning, revising and editing compositions is powerful (d = 0.82), particularly for struggling writers.
condition: especially for students who are struggling writers

statement: Writing gains come from summarizing strategies (d = 0.82), collaborative planning, drafting, revising and editing (d = 0.75), and setting clear specific goals for the product (d = 0.70), ahead of word processing (d = 0.55) and sentence-complexity strategies (d = 0.50).

Effective writing instruction for students with learning disabilities rests on explicit teaching of the critical steps of the writing process, the conventions of the genre, and guided feedback, with procedural prompts especially strong (d = 0.86).

Writing feedback works best when combined with instruction on the writing process or text structure, because that creates a shared vocabulary letting teacher and student discuss the work, and prompts give the responder concrete suggestions.
condition: when feedback accompanies instruction in the writing process or text structure

statement: Successful writing workshops share the use of teams, peer feedback and collaborative authorship, and their effect may derive from writing for a real and immediate audience or from needing to collaborate to finish the task.
The purpose of each piece of writing should be made explicit in the lesson, since audience and purpose appear to drive the gains from workshop and inquiry writing methods.

Creative drama used as an instructional tool produces d = 0.48 on cognitive skill acquisition and is more effective at preschool and elementary levels than with older children, benefiting both regular and remedial students.
condition: principally at preschool and elementary levels

statement: The mechanisms proposed for music practice improving reading — tonal sensitivity transferring to phonological sensitivity, predictable lyrics training reading, group music instilling responsibility — are plausible, but causality cannot be determined from the meta-analytic evidence.

The association between listening to music and spatial-temporal reasoning (d = 0.49) is remarkably variable, at best temporary, and of no established educational importance, so it should not be used to justify instructional practice.

Transfer from arts study occurs only across a narrow bridge — from visual arts experience to drawing-based tests — and not across a wide bridge to generating ideas, concepts or words, so narrow transfer must not be generalized to broad cognitive gain.

Very large reported effects for music (d = 2.90) come substantially from therapy rather than education studies, so a pooled effect must be checked for setting before it is read as an instructional result.

Music works as a behavioural contingency — slightly better at increasing desirable behaviour than reducing undesirable — and music interruption is more effective than music initiation for establishing that contingency.
Playing background music during mathematics tests has only a small positive effect, plausibly arousal rather than learning.

The relation between studying the arts and achievement is very small (d = 0.10) and non-causal; the plausible route is that arts study raises engagement in schooling, which in turn raises achievement.

Mathematics innovations produce their largest effects with lower-ability rather than higher-ability students, when the aid reduces cognitive load, and when feedback flows both from teacher to student and student to teacher.

In mathematics the highest effects come from teachers giving students feedback data or recommendations (d = 0.71), explicit teacher-led and direct instruction (d = 0.65 each) and peer-assisted learning (d = 0.62), while emphasizing real-world applications is the lowest (d = -0.04).

Giving teachers and students specific information on how each student is performing consistently enhances mathematics achievement — the single most consistent finding across mathematics interventions.
Modern mathematics, built on real-world relevance and heavy manipulative use, produces only d = 0.24 overall, with effects on application near zero (d = 0.06) despite its relevance rationale.
Manipulative materials in mathematics do not detract from learning but do little to support it, and their highest effects are on concrete rather than abstract instructional components.

In high school algebra the greatest effects come from direct instruction (d = 0.55) and problem solving (d = 0.52), and the lowest from technology-aided and communication or study-skills methods (d = 0.07 each).

Direct instruction outperforms alternatives because it focuses on desired learning outcomes, makes deliberate decisions about pacing and curriculum emphasis, and seeks enhanced learning for all students — not because it is didactic.

For learning-disabled and lower-achieving mathematics students the strongest programs are guided practice (d = 0.86), strategy-based methods (d = 0.85), peer tutoring (d = 0.76) and teacher modeling (d = 0.73); the weakest are working within a peer group (d = 0.15) and technology for independent practice (d = 0.16).
condition: for learning-disabled and lower-achieving students

statement: Peer tutoring (d = 0.76) far outperforms simply working within a peer group (d = 0.15), so structured tutoring and unstructured group work must not be treated as the same intervention.

Calculators warrant use when applied to computation, drill and checking; when they reduce cognitive load so students can attend to mathematical concepts; and when they are an integral pedagogical element rather than an add-on.
condition: when integrated into the teaching process for a stated pedagogical purpose

statement: Calculator effects are greatest for lower-ability students (d = 0.30) and negative for high-ability students (d = -0.23), because the cognitive-load relief they provide is redundant for students not constrained by computation.
exception: for high-ability students, where the effect is negative

statement: Calculator effects are much higher when the calculator is part of the teaching process — d = 0.72 for composition problem solving — than when merely present.
condition: when the calculator is embedded in instruction rather than merely available

statement: Allowing calculators during instruction but withholding them at test produces negative effects (d = -0.21), so the assessment condition must match the instructional condition.
Calculators are neither help nor hindrance to overall mathematics achievement; their minimum contribution is reduced cognitive load and improved student attitude to mathematics (d = 0.37).

Graphing-calculator effects are larger for conceptual (d = 0.72) than procedural (d = 0.52) skills, and calculator benefits do not vary by socioeconomic status, gender, grade, ability, ethnicity or prior calculator expertise.

Calculator gains in problem solving arise from improved computation and lowered cognitive workload, and the associated attitude gain likely comes from relieving students' dislike of word problems by removing the need to compute while solving.

Directive teaching makes the difference in mathematics: feedback, direct instruction, strategy-based methods, high challenge and mastery drive learning, while manipulatives and calculators serve only to free attention for problem solving.

Skills-based science programs emphasizing analytic and process skills outperform traditional fact-and-law curricula on attitudes, process skills, analytic skills and achievement, with positive effects on all outcomes except self-concept.
New science curricula help in life sciences, general science, physics and biology but not in chemistry or earth science, so the subject discipline conditions the effect.
exception: in chemistry and earth science, where effects are least positive

statement: Laboratory work used to question, explain and discover outperforms laboratory work used to verify previously presented material by d = 0.57, so the purpose of the lab, not the lab itself, carries the effect.
