Fewer than ten hours of computer pre-training is not merely unproductive but counterproductive, with those classes achieving substantially less than the average computer-using class, while more than ten hours yields up to 72 percent additional gain.
exception: training under ten hours, which produces worse-than-average outcomes

statement: Computer training should be concentrated rather than spread out: effects fall from d = 0.67 for courses under 4 weeks to d = 0.32 for courses over 14 weeks.
condition: when the required hours are concentrated into a few weeks

statement: Among computer uses, structured tutorials produce the greatest effect (d = 0.71), followed by programming (0.50) and word processing (0.42), while drill and practice (0.34), simulations (0.34) and problem solving (0.26) are lower.
Computer packages may be of better instructional quality than many teachers' methods because they are designed to be versatile enough to work across a range of subjects and settings.
Drill is a euphemism for practice — repeated learning until the material is mastered — and it is the key ingredient in mastery learning and deliberate practice, so students do need much of it.

Practice need not be dull: making deliberate practice engaging and worthwhile is a key teacher skill, and the drill attributes producing the highest effects are learner control, not losing sight of the learning goal, and immediate announcement of correctness.

Computer games demonstrate that repetitive drill with increasing challenge can be motivating, and computer drill and practice routines are frequently more effective than traditional teaching — which should prompt teachers to ask why.

Computer effects are greater when the student controls pacing, time allocation for mastery, sequencing, choice of practice items and reviewing than when the teacher or the system controls them (learner-controlled d = 0.41 against system-controlled d = -0.02).
condition: when the learner rather than teacher or system regulates the technology

statement: Students using word processors write more and better, especially the weaker writers, make more revisions and fewer errors, and length and quality are highly positively related so the extra output is not padding (d = 0.40).
Using computers in pairs is much more effective than alone or in larger groups (pairs d = 0.54 to 0.96 against individuals 0.25 to 0.56 and larger groups 0.39).
Groups that grow too large reduce each student's opportunity to explore beliefs and hypotheses and allow dominant members to crowd out submissive ones, lowering learning.

Students learning in pairs at computers show more positive peer interaction (d = 0.33), better use of task strategies (d = 0.50) and more perseverance (d = 0.48), while those working alone request more teacher help (d = 0.67) and finish faster.
Small-group computer learning is significantly enhanced when students have prior group work experience or instruction and when specific cooperative learning strategies are used.
condition: when students have group-work training and explicit cooperative structures

statement: Heterogeneous computer groups (d = 1.15) far outperform homogeneous ones (d = 0.51), though both beat working alone.

Pairs are the right structure for system-controlled close-ended tutorial or practice programs, whereas exploratory programs and general-purpose tools require emphasis on discussion so each member articulates and explains alternative hypotheses.

Computer feedback responds to every student regardless of who they are and is potentially less threatening and more programmed, which matters because teachers' claimed flexibility in deciding when and to whom to give feedback leaves many students without any.
In computer feedback, explanations (d = 0.66) and remediation (d = 0.73) are far more effective than simply providing the correct answer (d = -0.11).

Computer tasks must be challenging: effects are positive for challenging tasks (d = 0.13) but negative for moderately challenging (d = -0.34) and non-challenging ones (d = -0.57), so there is no point running computer-assisted activities without challenge.
condition: only when the task poses genuine challenge

statement: The three principles behind the highest computer-assisted instruction effects are that the teacher uses it to manage learner attention and motivation, to present new content and learning strategies, and to guide practice and active involvement — though that synthesis rests on only 13 studies.
The seven principles of good online-learning practice yield very small effects (d = 0.07 to 0.14), highest for encouraging student-faculty contact and lowest for emphasizing time on task.

Teaching students to look up encyclopedias and over-learn details is far less relevant than teaching them Boolean searching, evaluating the credibility of knowledge, and synthesizing the information available to them.

Web-based learning averages only d = 0.18 to 0.24 with huge variability and is generally much lower than other computer-based interventions, partly because it often ignores instructional design fundamentals such as interaction and timely feedback.
The web-based learning estimate rests on a new field whose early adopters were often faculty untrained in instructional design, so its average may shift as more studies accumulate.
Interactive video effect sizes are not homogeneous, so achievement from it depends on the instructional content, environment, method and materials rather than the medium.

Program-controlled interactive video appears more effective than learner-controlled, and group instruction advantages plausibly reflect teacher decisions about amount of practice, extent and kind of feedback, and remediation procedures.

A multimedia curriculum based on video games produced very low effects in both mathematics (d = 0.13) and language arts (d = 0.18) and in both high and low quality implementations, so implementation fidelity did not rescue it.

Visualization in interactive video (d = 0.71) conveys the essence of the message, illustrated materials beat verbal descriptions especially with high school students, and colour illustrations beat black and white.
Multimedia influence drops markedly when the design overloads visual or verbal working memory, so the teacher or text must help students connect verbal explanations to visual ones.
exception: when the presentation overloads visual or verbal working memory

statement: Students should receive both visual and verbal materials, because verbal material alone leaves an impoverished visual mental model insufficient to integrate with the verbal one.

Hypermedia beats traditional instruction more when delivered by regular class teachers than specialists, in elementary rather than high school, and when it supplements rather than substitutes for regular instruction.
condition: when used as a supplement to traditional learning

statement: Visual and audio-visual media produce very small or negative effects — television d = 0.05, film d = -0.07, tapes d = -0.27, slides d = -0.47 — and audiotapes of lessons do not move achievement, course evaluations or completions.

Simulation and gaming has only a small positive effect over alternative techniques (d = 0.12 to 0.38), somewhat larger against lectures alone (d = 0.32), and much larger on attitude (d = 0.64) than on achievement.

Shorter simulation interventions of up to one week are more effective than longer ones, and simulations work better with lower than higher ability students in one synthesis while another finds them better in higher grades.

Science simulations move surface outcomes more when used to confirm what was taught (d = 0.44) than when students explore freely (d = 0.27), but for deeper thinking outcomes the two approaches do not differ.
condition: for surface outcomes, where confirmatory use is stronger

statement: Simulation effects in colleges (d = 0.49) are far greater than in K-12 (d = 0.14), and simulations show no effect on attitudes or on retention two weeks later.

Programmed instruction consistently ranks near the bottom of method comparisons, below tutoring, computer-assisted instruction, Keller's system and audio-tutorials, and there is no support for students enjoying it.
The one synthesis finding a respectable programmed-instruction effect (d = 0.40) used only older students who were more self-regulating, which is the likely explanation rather than the method.
There is no difference in outcomes between distance and face-to-face students, which is not the same as distance education not working — the medium is not the message.
Web-delivered K-12 distance programs match traditional classrooms (d = 0.15) with no moderation by content, grade, school type, frequency, pacing, timing, instructor preparation or student setting.
Both synchronous (d = -0.10 to -0.02) and asynchronous (d = 0.05 to 0.06) distance education produce zero effects on achievement and negative to zero effects on attitude and retention.
The medium of instruction does not matter; how it is used to support instruction and facilitate learning is what affects outcomes.
Once the technology of a synchronous distance program was working and paid for, the remaining difference in outcomes was attributable to the quality of the teaching.

Whether and how much students interact with peers and instructors is the differentiating quality of distance programs, which explains why post-1998 studies with interaction facilities differ from earlier ones.

Technology-based home-school programs produce small effects on reading (d = 0.10), mathematics (d = 0.18) and writing (d = 0.34), with little evidence of enhanced home-school communication or parental involvement affecting learning.

Homework effects are twice as large for high school as junior high, and twice as large again for junior high as elementary (elementary d = 0.15 against high school d = 0.64), reflecting the more advanced study skills of older students.
For elementary students the correlation between time spent on homework and achievement is near zero (d = -0.04), so homework quantity at that level buys nothing.
Homework effects are negatively related to the duration of the homework treatment — shorter is better — and short, frequent, closely monitored homework is what the evidence favours.

Homework works best when it involves rote learning, practice or rehearsal of subject matter and the material is not complex; homework requiring higher-level conceptual thinking or project work is the least effective.
condition: when the task is practice or rehearsal of non-complex material
exception: for higher-level conceptual or project-based tasks, which are least effective as homework

statement: Deep learning homework fails because it needs the teaching cycle of learning, feedback and monitoring, whereas rehearsal of surface knowledge can proceed with minimal teacher supervision.

Parent support for autonomous student behaviour relates positively to achievement while direct instructional involvement by parents relates negatively, so the kind of parental help matters more than its presence.
A lot of homework combined with a lack of monitoring indicates an ineffective teaching method, and unmonitored homework can undermine motivation and let students internalize incorrect routines.
It would probably be more effective to run these practice opportunities under a teacher's gaze in the school rather than assign them as homework.
For many students homework reinforces that they cannot learn by themselves, undermining motivation and embedding less effective study habits, especially at elementary level.
Prescribing homework does not help students develop time management skills — there is no evidence this occurs — so that common justification is unsupported.

Homework effects are lower at elementary level partly because younger children are less able to ignore irrelevant stimulation, have less effective study habits, and receive little support from teachers or parents.
Homework in which the teacher has no active involvement does not contribute to student learning, just as technologies such as distance learning show no major effect without teacher involvement.

Resources such as adjunct aids and computers add value by diversifying teaching strategies, providing alternative practice opportunities, and increasing feedback to learner and teacher — but only once teachers have learned to optimize their use.
condition: when teachers have learned how to optimize the resource's use

statement: Interventions produce lower effects when delivered as part of comprehensive top-down teaching reforms, because teachers then do not evaluate whether the reform is working for them.

Commitment to the teaching strategy and re-learning how to use it through professional development are what make a method work, since it is differences in teachers that make the difference in student learning.

Many strategies work by reducing cognitive load so students can focus on the critical aspects of learning, which is particularly useful when they also get multiple opportunities for deliberate practice.

A synthesis of meta-analyses is a literature review whose contribution is a model, not an average of studies; presenting screeds of data would be the number-crunching that meta-analysis is criticized for.
The obsession with evidence-based decision making too often ignores the lens researchers use to decide what counts as evidence, what to exclude, and how the evidence is marshalled into a story.
The term effect size implies causation, but that causal claim is often not defensible; the harder and more valuable task is providing explanation rather than determining causality.
Synthesis of this kind is abductive rather than inductive or deductive: it offers inferences to the best explanation, and the resulting story should be bold enough to be potentially disprovable.

The core account is the power of passionate accomplished teachers who focus on students' cognitive engagement with the content, developing ways of thinking, reasoning, problem solving and strategies within that content.
Feedback comes second in the learning equation: monitoring, assessing and evaluating progress is what makes feedback powerful, so it presupposes the imparting of knowledge it evaluates.

Feedback runs both ways: to students it addresses what they already understand, misunderstand and construct; to teachers it addresses what the teacher understands, misunderstands and constructs about the learning of their students.

Learning is never linear: it requires learning and over-learning, dollops of feedback, much deliberate practice, many errors and mis-directions, and both accommodating and assimilating prior knowledge.
Teachers are among the most powerful influences in learning and need to be directive, influential, caring and actively engaged in the passion of teaching and learning.

Teachers need to know what each student is thinking and knowing, construct meaningful experiences in light of that, and hold enough content knowledge to give feedback that moves each student progressively through the curriculum levels.

Teachers need to know their lessons' learning intentions and success criteria, how well every student is attaining them, and where to go next given the gap — the three questions Where are you going, How are you going, Where to next.
Teaching must move from a single idea to multiple ideas and then relate and extend them, because what is critical is not the knowledge or ideas but the learner's construction of them.

School leaders and teachers need to create school, staffroom and classroom environments where error is welcomed as a learning opportunity, discarding incorrect knowledge is welcomed, and participants feel safe to learn, re-learn and explore.

The unit is teachers plural: teachers meeting to discuss, evaluate and plan their teaching in light of feedback evidence about their strategies — critical reflection in light of evidence, not critical reflection alone.

The signposts make no claim about additional structural resources, class size, which students are present, which subject is taught, or between-school differences, because effective teaching works similarly for all students, ethnicities and subjects.
Working conditions for teachers and students have small but positive effects, and positive means those conditions should not be made worse even though improving them is not the lever.

Under a decade-long voucher-type system the disparity between top and bottom schools increased dramatically, with parents fleeing schools with high minority proportions rather than moving toward higher measured outcomes, which were not even published.
Children from more advantaged families were the major beneficiaries of the voucher system and its loudest advocates, so school choice redistributed rather than raised quality.

Teachers' beliefs and conceptions must be subjected to debate, refutation and investigation — not because they are wrong but because that subjection is the essence of good teaching and the precondition for major achievement gains.
Teaching conceptions to interrogate include deciding what to teach next without attending to what students already know, and choosing materials with no evidence beyond prior use.
It is the effort a task elicits, not its interest level, that matters, so asking what activity provokes the most interest is the wrong question.
Teachers should maximize the challenge of learning goals and build structures for students to learn via that challenge, rather than structuring material so it is easy to learn.
Keeping students engaged and busy is not the same as ensuring they learn, and confusing the two is a defective conception of teaching.
The progress benchmark per implementation or year should be d = 0.40 for every student, at least d = 0.30, and certainly not less than d = 0.20.

Accomplished teachers should be defined as those who systematically make these differences — engaging students, turning them on to the subject, inspiring them and communicating a passion for learning.
Some learning is dull and repetitive and must be over-learned to free cognitive resources for anticipation and understanding; turning students on to that part of learning requires the same passion.
Teachers and principals should collect the effect sizes within their own schools and ask what is working best, why it is working best, and who it is not working for.
The attributes that work for student learning also work for teachers' learning: a caring supportive staffroom, tolerance of errors, and a peer culture of engagement, trust and shared passion.

Trust does not directly affect student learning but fosters organizational conditions: it reduces teachers' vulnerability when taking on uncertain reform tasks, facilitates innovation and public problem solving, and creates commitment to implementing successful innovations.

Schools that later proved academically improving reported higher levels of trust than non-improving ones (d = 0.61 reading, d = 0.64 mathematics), and trust maximizes the occurrence of error so feedback can be powerful.
The current penchant for reflective teaching too often ignores that reflection must rest on evidence rather than on post-hoc justification.
It is students, not teachers, who in the end decide what students will learn, so teachers must attend to what students are thinking, what their goals are, and why they would want to engage.

Learning being personal does not mean individualized instruction is needed; it means being aware of each student's progression, how they learn alone, with others and with adults, and what they bring from home and culture.

A classroom contains three worlds — the public world of teacher-led discussion and tasks, the private-social world of peer whispers and notes, and the private-individual world of self-talk — each with its own patterns, rules and discourse.

Classroom observation misses up to 40 percent of what occurs among students, which is why individual audio monitoring was needed and why critical reflection by teachers is barely adequate as a data source.

Students already know at least 40 percent of what teachers intend them to learn, a third of what each student learns is learned by no other student in the class, and a quarter of the concepts learned depend on private peer talk or self-designed activity.
Students learn how and when the teacher will notice them and how to give the appearance of active involvement, so visible engagement is not evidence of learning.
Teachers know very little about what is going on in their classrooms, which is why learning outcomes feel unpredictable, mysterious and uncontrollable to them.

In most teachers' minds the criteria for successful learning are the same as the criteria for successful classroom management, so they read enthusiasm, puzzlement and questions as evidence that teaching is going well.

Although the activity is supposed to produce learning, neither teachers nor students talk about learning: teachers talk about resources, how long an activity should take, and what happens if it is unfinished.

Teachers depend on the responses of a small number of key students as indicators and remain ignorant of what most of the class knows and understands, sustained by the belief that engagement in appropriate activities implies learning.
Asked what they were thinking, students most commonly reported thinking about how to finish quickly or how to reach the answer with the least possible effort.

Regardless of prior ability, students who used the classroom to further their own interests and purposes learned more than those who dutifully did what they were told but could not create their own opportunities.

It takes three or four experiences of interacting with relevant information — not simple repetitions but different ways of coming at the material — for a knowledge construct to form in working memory and transfer to long-term memory.
Distributing practice across different days rather than grouping learning episodes within a single day greatly improves the amount of material retained over sizeable periods.

Students who cannot participate in a learning activity for cultural or ethnic reasons not only miss the knowledge they need but learn that their ability to acquire knowledge is inferior, a deficit belief teachers can reinforce by sharing it.
Teachers should focus on direct observation of the realities of student experience and build a precise, accurate and replicable account of both the subjective and objective sides of it.
The teacher as activator averages d = 0.60 while the teacher as facilitator averages d = 0.17, so active and guided instruction is much more effective than unguided facilitative instruction.

Activator strategies include reciprocal teaching (0.74), feedback (0.72), self-verbalization and meta-cognition (0.67), Direct Instruction (0.59) and mastery learning (0.57); facilitator strategies include simulations (0.32), inquiry teaching (0.31), smaller classes (0.21), problem-based learning (0.15) and whole language (0.06).

Minimally guided methods rest on two assumptions — that learners construct their own solutions to authentic problems, and that knowledge is best acquired through the discipline's procedures — and each new wave of advocates seems unaware of or uninterested in the prior evidence that they have not been validated.
Students preferred less guided methods yet learned less from them, so student preference is not a valid basis for choosing an instructional method.
Constructivism is a form of knowing, not a form of teaching, and constructing conceptual knowledge must not be confused with constructivism as a teaching fad.

If constructivism means treating learners as active, their learning as socially constructed, and requiring them to create or recreate knowledge for themselves, then the more direct and active teaching methods are optimal for achieving it.
The only way constructive thinking applies to teaching is to the teachers themselves, who construct conceptions, beliefs and models about how they teach and how students learn.

Direct, actively involved teaching with a high sense of agency leads to higher levels of learning, autonomy and self-regulation in the learner — the very outcomes unguided methods claim as their rationale.
Active quality teaching strategies average d = 0.68 against d = 0.08 for working conditions, so structures and conditions are not where the leverage lies.
Educational structures such as tracking, class size, school mix and finances have only indirect or probabilistic effects on learning, mediated by instructional and peer processes.

Reducing class size does not directly influence learning; it merely raises the probability that the environment can be structured to capitalize on teaching and peer influences, and in practice teachers often change nothing about interactions, curricula or strategies.

Almost all state and federal policy addresses structural issues — resources, class size, choice, curriculum, tests and high-stakes assessment — and it is rare to find a policy that relates to teaching.

It is less the methods themselves than the principles of effective teaching and learning that matter; a low-effect method such as team teaching (d = 0.19) could produce much greater effects if run with attention to student-teacher feedback and challenging goals.

The prescription trap warns that a prescribed teaching package works mainly where teachers are poorly prepared and there is a history of failure and disorder, is hard to maintain, and may leave students dependent when they meet new tasks.

What makes the difference is not a particular method or script but personalizing the learning, gaining precision about how students are progressing, and ensuring teachers keep learning how and when to use different strategies.

Teaching influences average d = 0.68 — quality of teaching 0.77, reciprocal teaching 0.74, teacher-student relationships and feedback 0.72 — against d = 0.08 for working conditions, where retention (-0.16) and summer vacation classes (-0.09) are negative.

Active teaching must not be confused with transmission or frontal instruction, which pitches at middle to high achievers while pacing on feedback from low achievers, so fast achievers are under-stimulated and low achievers frustrated.

Transmission teaching leads teachers to seek more engaging rather than more challenging tasks, more frontal talk and questions they already know the answers to, and leaves students believing progress depends on teacher-directed methods.

Active teaching uses backward design: start from the desired results — success criteria tied to learning intentions — rather than from textbooks, favoured lessons and time-honoured activities, then evaluate those materials against the goals.

The aim of teaching is to get students to learn the skills of teaching themselves — to develop explicit cognitive schemas, self-regulate, and understand why they need to invest in deliberate practice.
Learning strategies enable progress through the three worlds of surface, deep and constructed understanding, and reduce cognitive load by over-learning surface information so heuristics can develop.

The most important precondition for deliberate practice is that it be embedded in a higher-order set of learnings, because practice unrelated to more challenging goals is dull, repetitive and counter to engagement.
condition: when the practice is embedded in a higher-order learning goal

statement: Other preconditions for effective deliberate practice include awareness of learning intentions and goals, advance organizers, worked examples, and pre-practice briefing and orientation.
Students arrive with preconceptions about how the world works, and teachers must engage that initial understanding or students may fail to grasp the new concepts and information.

Developing competence requires students to have a deep foundation of factual knowledge, to understand ideas within a conceptual framework, and to organize knowledge so it can be retrieved and applied.
A meta-cognitive approach to instruction helps students take control of their own learning by defining learning goals and monitoring their progress toward them.
Prior knowledge can stand in the way of new learning, so students must learn how to resolve internal inconsistencies and restructure existing conceptions when necessary.

Learning requires the active involvement of the learner, is primarily a social activity, builds on what is already understood and believed, and takes considerable time and practice to start building expertise.

Teachers need to be adaptive learning experts with enough flexibility to innovate when routines are not enough: able to tell when students are not learning, know where to go next, adapt resources and strategies, and alter the classroom climate.
Adaptive experts know how to continuously expand their expertise, restructuring their knowledge and competencies to meet new challenges.

Teachers need cognitive and affective empathy — hearing the intent and emotion behind what a student says and reflecting it back by paraphrasing — and must attend to how children define, describe and interpret problems from their own perspective.

Challenging learning intentions induce students to invest greater effort and more of their total capacity than low-demand conditions do, and the rate of learning is a direct function of goal difficulty.
Students must know a goal before they can commit to it, and exhortations to do your best rarely sustain interest in learning.
Challenging goals increase the need for and effectiveness of feedback: if the goal is easy feedback is unnecessary, if difficult the need for feedback is greater.
condition: when the goal is difficult rather than easy

statement: Feedback tells people what is and goals tell them what is desirable; feedback involves information and goals involve evaluation, and together they are the joint effect of motivation and cognition controlling action.
Evidence does not provide rules for action but only hypotheses for intelligent problem solving and for inquiring into the ends of education.
What works? by itself is a barren question; the questions that must be explored are what works best, compared to what alternatives, when, for whom, and to what ends.
The constant need to ask what the desirable outcomes of any teaching are, alongside teachers' judgment proficiency and caring relationships, points to the moral dimensions of teaching.
Any recommendation about what works best invokes cultural claims: classrooms enact individualism, community or collectivism, and these values drive interaction and discourse patterns.

In British and American classrooms mistakes are treated as embarrassing and minimized to save face, with emphasis on correct answers and teacher approval, whereas Russian classrooms put problems and mistakes in the public domain to be engaged with.

Across seven countries mathematics lessons look consistent: students solve problems alone or in whole-class groups rather than small peer groups, textbooks and worksheets are used extensively, and teachers talk eight times more than students.
Reducing a classroom to an effect-size index is like reducing a society to unemployment or intelligence indices, and the classic cautions about index numbers apply.

When reading an effect size, the variability around it can be as informative as the typical value, the unexplained variance limits the importance of the explained variance, the reference point is critical, and interactions with other variables can dramatically alter the conclusion.
Rival plausible hypotheses are the most important consideration in any discussion of indices; the visible-teaching story is one plausible model to fit these data and alternatives are welcomed.
Differential effects by school subject were hard to find: good teaching and the most powerful influences on outcomes seem similar across domains, which undercuts high-school subject chauvinism.
There was no preponderance of evidence supporting the importance of subject knowledge or pedagogical content knowledge for student outcomes.

The rarely explored content knowledge that may matter more is the teacher's conception of progress in the subject, knowledge of when to intervene, knowledge of learning theory, and openness to alternative ways to teach the content.

Achievement has three levels — surface, deep, and conceptual or constructed understanding — alongside other critical outcomes such as fluency, retention, application, endurance and problem-solving strategies.

Most tests used in these studies measure surface features effectively, deep learning somewhat, and the constructed representations students build rarely — so the book's results speak more to surface and deep knowing than to conceptual understanding.
At the constructed level knowing is an activity, not a thing: it is reciprocally constructed in the individual-environment-teacher interaction and not easily captured by a one-off test.
The standard for minimal success should be d = 0.40 rather than the zero point, and that hinge-point is the average rather than the maximum attainable effect.

Progress is too often cast in terms of activities and events, or in terms of test scores, rather than in terms of increasingly challenging demands from the underlying concepts and the proficiencies those scores supposedly measure.

Comparing this year's achievement to last year's and concluding that it worked, that no one complained, or that weaker students reflect what they brought to class are among the weakest of all evidence claims.

Going backwards covers not only students who fall behind their starting point but those who miss the expected yearly gain and those who fall short of what they could achieve because their teachers hold low expectations.

In some schools 80 percent of students went backwards in a year, notably in grade 9 mathematics where students first meet algebra, disengage, form beliefs about their low performance and often drop the subject.
Asking teachers what percentage of their students go backwards in a year with them is rarely considered, which reduces the chance of teachers finding those students before the problems compound.
Referencing success to the zero point is why it is hard to find a below-average teacher, why every teacher is considered effective, and why all can claim to have added value.
One of the greatest myths of teaching is that all teachers are equal; there is appreciable variability in teacher effectiveness, evidenced by how little variance lies between schools.

About 40 percent of students report going through the motions, trying neither hard nor paying attention; about half who drop out say classes were not interesting and two-thirds say no teacher was interested in their success.

The teachers students remember are those who cared about teaching them a passion for the subject, gave them confidence in themselves as learners and people, treated them as a person, and instilled a love of learning — not those who covered a syllabus.

Good intentions fall short because decisions are inappropriately compared, inadequately evaluated against alternatives, aimed at structural and working conditions rather than teaching strategies, and evaluated by models that seek success and ignore failure.
The typical teacher effect is about d = 0.15 to 0.35; effects rise markedly beyond that only when there is an intervention or innovation.

Innovation does not mean novelty: it occurs when a teacher deliberately introduces a method, curriculum or strategy different from what they currently use, and change for the sake of change is not what is needed.
Teachers should construe their teaching as a series of related experimental designs, so the benefits of increased attention to outcomes can be accrued.

The critical change agents in therapy, in order, are knowledge and skills, a plan of action, strategies to overcome setbacks, a high sense of confidence, monitoring progress, commitment to achieve, social and environmental support, and last, freedom, control or choice.

The most critical attribute of an innovation is not the innovation itself but the heightened attention to its effects, the feedback to the teacher about those effects, and the focus on its learning intentions and success criteria.
An innovation usually changes during implementation, so what is evaluated at the end is not what was initiated.
The desirable lens of success is in place when teachers seek evidence that their teaching may not have been successful, because we otherwise see evidence of our success everywhere.

Disconfirmation must be sought at every level: teaching may fail for some students, for parts of the learning intentions, or against aspects of the success criteria, and the goals, challenge level and engagement processes all need constant questioning.
Teachers are willing to change but are sick of change, because most changes they experience target structural and working conditions rather than their own conceptions of teaching and learning.

Changing conceptions requires openness to the idea and a willingness to be wrong — seeking a better alternative by evaluating the change's effect on student learning — because adopting an innovation means discontinuing a familiar practice.
The key issue is less how to change than why we do not, so diagnosis should target the reasons for non-change rather than the mechanics of change.

Beliefs persist despite not working through over-reliance on anecdotes, dressing beliefs in scientific or pedagogical jargon, bold claims, privileging one's own past experience as sufficient evidence, and circular reasoning of the form I am doing it so it must be fine.

The psychological processes sustaining current practice are the need for certainty, control and simplicity, seeking confirming examples, failing to seek evidence of what is not working, attributing failure to the student but success to the teacher, and immunity to different ideas.

Revolutionary teaching ideas are resisted rather than welcomed because every successful teacher has a vested intellectual, social and financial interest in the status quo — and welcoming every new idea would produce chaos.
Teaching is carried out largely out of sight and hearing of other teachers, so teachers rely on war stories and personal experience to construct shared understanding and justify their preferences.

Teacher narratives can become productive when teachers question one another, elicit replays and rehearsals, use evidence within the narratives, and offer and revise interpretations — building general principles anchored in both concepts and particulars.
condition: when the narrative is interrogated with evidence rather than merely swapped

statement: Evidence-sharing among teachers requires instructional leadership and a safe trusting environment for criticism, a commitment to share evidence about teaching effects, and openness to new experience.

The teacher's lens is critical to success and must be scrutinized, considered from another's viewpoint, and checked against evidence that all students are learning desirable outcomes at a sufficient rate.

Seeing learning through students' eyes means seeking countering evidence about one's teaching, looking for errors in one's own thinking, watching how students build on prior conceptions, asking whether challenge and engagement suffice, and understanding the strategies students use when they hit difficulty.
Statistical methods are somewhat more accurate than clinical or intuitive judgment across 173 effect sizes spanning 56 years, replicating a finding first established in the 1950s.

The repeated finding that statistical beats clinical judgment has had little influence on practice because practitioners lack familiarity with statistical methods, value interpersonal cues, believe statistics dehumanize, and recall their correct predictions but not their wrong ones.

Teachers measure success by the satisfaction of doing a good job and the approval of parents and principals rather than by student outcomes, because the incentive structure in schools does not emphasize student performance.

Of more than 5,000 children referred to school psychologists for failing, not one referral located the problem in a poor instructional program, poor school practice or a poor teacher; all were attributed to the home or located within the student.

A system that concludes all problems are caused by defects in the children and none by defects in the system is arrogant, and schools should be challenged to answer where the practice has produced effective results and where the data show superiority over successful programs rather than over the last failed attempt.

An innovation should be asked to show where it was installed with effective results, where teachers were trained to perform uniformly within its guidelines, and which historically successful teachers endorse it.

The closer an innovation gets to the core of schooling the less likely it is to influence teaching and learning at scale, while those furthest from teaching and learning are the ones most likely to become national policy.

Schools are constantly changing, so the problem is not general resistance to change; the resistance sits in the conceptions of teaching and learning shared by teachers, expressed as leave me alone to teach my way.
It is nearly impossible to legislate changes to conceptions of teaching and learning, which is what makes professional development critical and why most policy changes have little or no effect.
Policy churn is like a storm at sea: the surface is agitated and turbulent while the ocean floor stays calm and life goes on largely uninterrupted.

The class-size belief survives because listeners suspend belief in the contrary evidence and argue from probability — that smaller classes surely bring more feedback and individualization — but the interesting question is why those benefits do not accrue when class sizes fall.
A major area for educational research should be why we continue to believe claims about what works best when there is no evidence for them.

It is far easier to discuss and fund working conditions — class size, salary, buildings, longer days — or parent appeasements such as computers, school choice and more examinations, than to change the transmission model of teaching.
The operational demand should be that schools enhance learning by at least d = 0.30 more than last year and preferably more than d = 0.40 before an intervention is considered worth retaining.

Evidence is not neutral: what counts as effective depends on judgments about what is educationally desirable, and achievement is only one among other critical outcomes such as affective, persistence, physical and social outcomes.

Education is never neutral because its fundamental purpose is intervention or behaviour change, which makes teaching a moral profession facing questions such as why teach this rather than that and how to teach in defensible ways.

Teaching involves ethics in its aims, methods and relationships, requires respect for autonomy and for reason, and talk of the technicist, competent or skilled teacher should remind us that education is essentially a moral enterprise.
Only meta-analyses were given the privilege of inclusion here; a review of non-meta-analytic and qualitative studies could yield a richer and more nuanced statement of the evidence.
Evidence based on effect sizes alone can lead to poor decisions, because every choice has costs as well as benefits and the financial cost of an intervention may need to enter the comparison.

Education costs come in distinct forms — cost-minimization, cost-benefit trade-off, and average versus incremental cost-effectiveness, the last being the cost of switching from the current practice to another.

The most critical costs are opportunity costs — students losing access to activities that truly make a difference and which their peers are benefiting from — and the suffering costs of exposure to the least effective interventions.
That a teacher has used an intervention before, enjoys it, or can find anecdotal support for it does not offset the suffering cost of a low-effectiveness intervention.

Vast sums are invested in educational innovations, changes and policies without much evidence that the investment moves student outcomes, though it may improve teachers' and students' working conditions.

Schools that doubled performance set high goals such as 90 to 95 percent proficiency, analyzed student data deeply, used formative assessment, collectively reviewed evidence on good instruction, used time productively, and had instructional leadership.
Increasing the share of spending on instruction is unlikely by itself to affect student learning, since 60 percent already goes there.

Educational production shows diminishing marginal returns: doubling learning time does not double outcomes, and adding more influences and methods can lead to fewer outcomes than choosing the optimal smaller set.
The effects reported are unlikely to be additive: coupling interventions together does not mean their effects can be summed, and the Adventure-program additivity was noted as unusual.
exception: a few cases such as home plus school effects and adventure programs, where additivity was observed

statement: What matters is the right combination of interventions in the right proportions to produce an interaction effect, not the accumulation of individually effective methods.

Halving class size from 30 to 15 yields only d = 0.10 to 0.20, and the true cost includes not just staffing but extra classrooms, resources, ongoing professional development and finding the additional qualified teachers.
The right question about a resource is what is the best use of it, or what could be accomplished if the money were spent on innovations with higher effects on student outcomes.

To match the achievement benefit of increased textbook availability at equal cost, schools would have to cut average class size from 40 to 10, so lowering class size to raise achievement is in most situations not an efficient strategy.

Comparing four elementary reforms on cost-effectiveness, cross-age tutoring was the most cost-effective, computer-assisted instruction mid-range, and a longer school day and reducing class size by five students the smallest returns.

The reforms with most power over student learning are expensive, mostly in the effort costs of teachers, school leaders and students — costs too often assumed free or taken from teachers' social and home life.

Adoption of an innovation is a process rather than a discrete event, moving through awareness, knowledge, persuasion, decision, implementation and confirmation, with imprecise boundaries and not all phases occurring.

Diffusion starts with a few teachers who are open to change, more educated, self-confident and less concerned with others' norms; once a critical mass forms many more innovate, but the final fifth are very hard to reach.
Closing the deal on adoption requires interpersonal outreach: social networks are powerful but are often the biggest barrier to innovation.
Across two centuries of teaching, about 85 percent of teachers resist changing what they believe works, ten percent will change to be more efficient, and five percent will try new innovations.
Accountability, government pressure, compulsion and the stick rarely change the conceptions or lens of teachers.

Government agencies, departments and teacher educators demand that teachers be evidence-based while themselves being reluctant to accept evidence contrary to current policy, preferring changes to structural and working conditions.

Damage in schools is not confined to teachers with zero or negative gains; teachers and schools that do not aim for and reach the d = 0.40 hinge-point condemn their students to mediocrity and lesser opportunities.
The devil in this story is not the criminal or incompetent teacher but the average get-through-the-curriculum, behave, be busy teacher who has no idea of the damage being done.

In Project Follow Through, involving over 72,000 students across more than 180 sites over ten years, all but one program had close to zero or negative effects; only Direct Instruction produced positive effects on basic skills, deeper comprehension, social and affective measures.

Direct Instruction students followed to the end of schooling were twice as likely to graduate high school and scored higher in reading (d = 0.43) and mathematics (d = 0.28), showing significant long-term effects.

The outcome of Project Follow Through was not more implementation of the method that worked but more resources for the methods that did not, because the romantic view of students discovering learning outweighed a method requiring attention to detail and teaching specific skills.
Rejecting an evidenced method in favour of an ideologically preferred one is the mark of an immature profession that lacks a solid scientific base and has less respect for evidence than for opinion.

Medicine was once equally unscientific — treatments tried on trial and error lasting decades before being abandoned — and evidence-based practice was the mechanism that drove out dogma, since dogma does not destroy itself.

Medicine's evidence-based revolution came through pressure from groups adversely affected by poor service, so the analogous catalysts in education may be equity litigation, clinical trials of educational treatments, and international outcome standards.
The key question is whether teaching can shift from an immature to a mature profession — from opinions to evidence, from subjective judgment and personal contact to critique of judgments.
Effective elementary teachers devote most class time to academic activity that requires students to think as they read, write and discuss, rather than to activity that keeps students busy.

Effective teachers do explicit teaching and reteaching of skills — modeling and explaining, then guided student practice — and scaffolding and reteaching account for a large proportion of their effort.

Effective teachers strongly balance skills instruction with holistic reading and writing activities rather than choosing between them, and connect content learning in science, social studies and mathematics to reading and writing instruction.

Effective teachers hold high expectations and consistently ratchet academic demand — encouraging slightly more advanced books and slightly longer, more complex writing — rather than holding difficulty constant.
From the first day of school effective teachers communicate high expectations that students will self-regulate and take charge of their own behaviour and academic engagement.
Of thirteen dimensions distinguishing experienced experts from experienced non-experts, only three were needed to separate the groups: challenge, deep representation, and monitoring and feedback.
The effects of teaching expertise are greatest on deep understanding: 74 percent of certified teachers' student work was judged deep against 29 percent for non-certified teachers.
Experienced experts hold pedagogical content knowledge they employ more flexibly and innovatively, and can alter instruction in response to the contextual features of the classroom situation.
Experienced experts understand at a deeper level why an individual student succeeded or failed on a task and generate more accurate hypotheses about the causes of that success and failure.

Experienced experts set developmentally appropriate tasks that engage, challenge and intrigue students without boring or overwhelming them, anticipate the difficulties students will meet with new concepts, and improvise when things do not run smoothly.

Teachers who live these principles question themselves, worry about which students are not progressing appropriately, seek evidence of successes and gaps, and ask for help with their teaching when they need it.
The most effective teachers are often not the ones parents pick as better, but the students know them and welcome being in their classes.

Teaching should nurture and challenge intellectual and imaginative capacity out to horizons unsullied by self-fulfilling minimalist expectations, rather than patronize students with lowest-common-denominator content or crush their love of learning with boring pedagogy.

Schooling must not limit the exploration of evolving knowledge to repetitively recycled worksheets, and must ensure legitimate progression of learning from one day, week, month, term and year to the next.
Students should be taught with humanity and sensitivity as developing human beings worthy of genuine respect, enlightened discipline and imaginative flair.

Self-reported grades and student self-assessment of achievement produce the largest student-domain effects of all (d = 0.47 to 3.10 across syntheses), making student prediction of their own performance a top-ranked influence.

Prior achievement and prior ability are strong predictors of later achievement (d = 0.31 to 1.28, with high-school-to-university grade prediction at d = 0.90 to 1.02), so any intervention claim must be adjusted for prior attainment.

Personality contributes almost nothing to achievement (d = 0.06 to 0.10) while self-concept (0.32 to 0.41) and self-efficacy (0.37 to 0.76) contribute materially, so student traits and student beliefs must not be conflated.
Reducing anxiety raises achievement (d = 0.22 to 0.56), as does concentration and engagement (d = 0.48 to 1.09), while resilience programs for at-risk students show essentially nothing (d = 0.03).
Physical and dietary influences are weak: removing artificial food colours gives d = 0.12, relaxation d = 0.16, chronic illness absence d = 0.20, and physical fitness or exercise d = 0.25 to 0.36.

The 138 influences on achievement are rank-ordered by effect size from self-reported grades (d = 1.44) at the top to student mobility (d = -0.34) at the bottom, giving a single comparative barometer for judging any proposed intervention.

The top ten influences are self-reported grades (1.44), Piagetian programs (1.28), providing formative evaluation (0.90), micro teaching and acceleration (0.88), classroom behavioural interventions (0.80), comprehensive interventions for learning disabled students (0.77), teacher clarity (0.75), reciprocal teaching (0.74) and feedback (0.73).

Ranks 11 to 30 are dominated by teacher and teaching influences — teacher-student relationships (0.72), spaced practice (0.71), meta-cognitive strategies (0.69), self-questioning (0.64), professional development (0.62), problem-solving teaching and not labeling students (0.61), phonics and teaching strategies (0.60), study skills and Direct Instruction (0.59), mastery learning (0.58), worked examples (0.57).
Home environment (0.57) and socioeconomic status (0.57) rank alongside strong teaching influences at 31 and 32, while parental involvement is 45th (0.51) and home visiting 89th (0.29).

The d = 0.40 hinge-point falls around rank 64 to 66 — science (0.40), social skills programs (0.40) and reducing anxiety (0.40) — so roughly the top half of influences clear the benchmark and the rest do not.

Six influences are negative and should be avoided or mitigated: student mobility (-0.34), television (-0.18), retention or holding a student back (-0.16), welfare policies (-0.12) and summer vacation (-0.09).

The most commonly advocated structural levers rank in the bottom third: class size 106th (0.21), charter schools 107th (0.20), finances 99th (0.23), summer school 98th (0.23), ability grouping 121st (0.12) and open versus traditional classrooms 133rd (0.01).

Teacher training ranks 124th (0.11) and teacher subject matter knowledge 125th (0.09), while teacher clarity ranks 8th (0.75) and professional development 19th (0.62) — what teachers do outranks what teachers hold as credentials.

Technology influences cluster below the hinge-point: interactive video 44th (0.52) is the exception, while computer-assisted instruction is 71st (0.37), simulations 82nd (0.33), visual and audio-visual methods 104th (0.22), web-based learning 112th (0.18) and distance education 126th (0.09).

Grouping practices rank poorly throughout: small group learning 48th (0.49), ability grouping for gifted students 87th (0.30), within-class grouping 116th (0.16), ability grouping 121st (0.12) and multi-grade classes 131st (0.04).

Matching style of learning ranks 62nd (0.41) yet aptitude-treatment interactions rank 108th (0.19) and student control over learning 132nd (0.04), so the differentiation family of influences performs far worse than its advocacy suggests.

Fixed student attributes rank low — gender 122nd (0.12), personality 109th (0.19), diet 123rd (0.12), lack of illness 102nd (0.23) — against malleable student states such as concentration and engagement 49th (0.48) and motivation 51st (0.48).

Within the school domain the strongest influences are acceleration 5th (0.88) and classroom behavioural interventions 6th (0.80), well ahead of classroom cohesion 39th (0.53), classroom management 42nd (0.52) and school effects 50th (0.48).
Principals and school leaders rank 74th (0.36), below classroom-level influences, so leadership acts on learning indirectly rather than as a direct lever.

Within reading curricula the ranking is vocabulary and repeated reading 15th and 16th (0.67), phonics 22nd (0.60), comprehension programs 28th (0.58), exposure to reading 76th (0.36), sentence combining 119th (0.15) and whole language 129th (0.06).
Students comprehend new material by relating it to knowledge already stored in memory.
Before introducing related material, prompt every learner to retrieve relevant foundations and explicitly help them connect those foundations to the new content.
condition: When upcoming learning depends on relevant prior knowledge.

statement: When teaching through analogy, explain the mapped relationship, direct attention to the relevant similarities, and address misleading inferences.
condition: When an analogy is used to introduce an unfamiliar idea.
exception: Do not rely on an unexplained analogy or leave misconceptions induced by it uncorrected.

statement: Working memory has limited capacity and can be overloaded by excessive information or task demands.
Manage cognitive demand with carefully paced, explicit explanation, modeling, and examples.
condition: When content or a task could exceed learners' working-memory capacity.

statement: Coordinate visual and verbal information so the channels complement each other and avoid simultaneously presenting competing verbal streams.
condition: When using more than one presentation modality.
exception: Do not pair spoken explanation with different on-screen prose that divides attention.

statement: Include visual and descriptive details only when they clarify the target concept, because attention-grabbing decoration can distract from learning.
condition: When selecting supplementary details, stories, or visuals.

statement: Preteach essential concepts and vocabulary when doing so will reduce load and make relationships in the full lesson easier to understand.
condition: When unfamiliar prerequisite ideas or terms would impede the lesson.

statement: Use worked examples to expose the reasoning behind each step and connect procedures to underlying concepts.
condition: When learners need support with a new task or procedure.
exception: Do not let learners merely copy steps without explaining why they work.

statement: Judge readiness for content by mastery of its prerequisites rather than by a presumed age-linked developmental stage.
condition: When deciding whether a learner is ready for particular content.
exception: Do not withhold content solely because it is labeled developmentally inappropriate.

statement: Revisit important knowledge periodically after its initial lesson because one exposure does not produce durable learning.
Durable, usable knowledge requires learners to process meaning rather than merely encounter information in working memory.
Assign explanation and meaningful-organization tasks that make learners attend to relationships, causes, and connections with prior knowledge.
condition: When the goal is durable understanding rather than short-term completion.

statement: Teach a concept with multiple varied examples and require application across varied situations.
condition: When learners must abstract a concept beyond one example.

statement: Use a mnemonic as an organizational aid for difficult-to-recall information, not as a substitute for understanding its meaning.
condition: When essential information is otherwise hard to remember.

statement: Space practice over time, using shorter intervals for newly learned material and progressively longer intervals as mastery grows.
condition: When designing practice for long-term retention.

statement: Require every learner to produce an answer from memory through effortful but achievable retrieval rather than relying on volunteers or passive recognition.
condition: When practicing previously taught knowledge.
exception: Retrieval should not be so difficult that successful recall is implausible.

statement: Move from initially blocked practice to cumulative, spaced, and interleaved practice after learners have achieved initial fluency.
condition: When learners can already perform the new or complex problem type with initial fluency.
exception: For an unfamiliar or complex problem type, begin with blocked practice before interleaving.

statement: Make feedback clear, specific, explanatory, improvement-oriented, and focused on the task rather than personal traits.
condition: When responding to learner performance.

statement: Give immediate corrective feedback during targeted skill practice, but consider delayed feedback for already-proficient learners when retention is the goal.
condition: Feedback timing can be matched to the learning goal and the learner's proficiency.

statement: Use low-stakes, non-evaluative retrieval opportunities so practice strengthens memory without being treated as a high-stakes test.
condition: When the purpose is retrieval practice rather than assessment.

statement: Build systematic domain knowledge because fluent problem solving and apparently general skills depend on facts and vocabulary stored in long-term memory.
condition: When teaching problem solving or a general-seeming skill within a subject.
exception: Do not teach the skill as though it operates independently of domain knowledge.

statement: Transfer to a novel problem depends on knowledge of its context and recognition of its underlying structure; training in one domain does not automatically transfer to another.
condition: When a learned skill must be used in a new context.

statement: Have learners compare problems with different surface features but the same deep structure, and explicitly identify the shared structure.
condition: When teaching for transfer across problem contexts.

statement: Begin a new problem type with concrete, structured representations and gradually replace them with symbolic or abstract forms as understanding develops.
condition: When learners are moving from an example toward recognizing a problem's general structure.

statement: Use correct examples first for novices, then ask learners to explain correct, erroneous, and boundary-defining examples to deepen conceptual understanding.
condition: When learners have enough initial understanding to analyze why an example succeeds or fails.
exception: At the earliest learning stage, delay erroneous examples until correct examples are established.

statement: Provide structured worked examples to beginners and fade support toward independent problem solving as proficiency increases.
condition: When instruction can be adjusted to the learner's level of expertise.

statement: Teach multiple problem-solving strategies and interleave opportunities to select the strategy that fits each problem, including attention to efficiency after conceptual understanding is secure.
condition: When learners possess sufficient conceptual understanding to compare and choose strategies.

statement: Support motivation through meaningful attainable challenges, appropriate agency, clear expectations, individual-progress feedback, and policies that permit low-stakes practice and recovery.
condition: When designing the learning environment and its motivational signals.
exception: Choice should remain structured, relevant to the learning goal, and limited enough to avoid overload.

statement: Pair high expectations and constructive criticism with credible support and care, and keep classroom policies consistent with messages about learners' potential.
condition: When communicating expectations or corrective feedback.
exception: Do not undermine growth messages through harsh penalties for early errors, social comparison, or praise that signals low expectations.

statement: Use extrinsic incentives selectively for activities that lack intrinsic motivation because rewards can reduce existing interest.
condition: When learners are not already intrinsically motivated for the activity.
exception: Avoid adding controlling rewards to an activity learners already find intrinsically engaging.

statement: Build motivation through early, scaffolded success and belonging, but do not treat motivation as sufficient evidence that learning is occurring.
condition: When learners lack confidence, connection, or initial motivation.
exception: Sustained learning still requires effective acquisition and practice of knowledge and skills.

statement: Teach self-regulation as a recurring cycle of planning, monitoring, adjustment, and reflection, and prompt learners to choose strategies before supplying help.
condition: When developing learners' capacity to manage work independently.
exception: Do not withdraw necessary instructional support before learners have workable strategies and resources.

statement: Use delayed retrieval and explanation to monitor durable learning because immediate ease, error-free completion, and short-term performance can create false confidence.
condition: When learners or teachers are judging whether knowledge will be retained.
exception: Do not infer durable competence from cramming, blocked success, open notes, hints, or assignment completion alone.

statement: Structure collaborative work so individual contributions matter, the task requires participation from all members, the group is manageable, and roles are clear.
condition: When group work is intended to support belonging and meaningful learning.
exception: Unstructured collaboration can permit one learner to do the work for the group.

statement: Design difficult learning activities so the challenge is purposeful, matched to learners' current knowledge, and supported by a path toward progress.
condition: When using productive struggle or desirable difficulty.
exception: Increasing difficulty by itself does not improve learning.

statement: Build learning habits with routines that require effortful recall, are spaced over time, include feedback, and remain connected to meaningful content.
condition: When routines are used to sustain self-regulated learning without relying on momentary motivation.
exception: A routine performed mechanically for its own sake is not sufficient.

statement: Evidence does not support matching instruction to fixed learning-style or left-brain/right-brain categories; broadly effective strategies can support learners across such preferences.

Adapt instruction as expertise develops: novices benefit more from worked examples, blocked practice, shorter spacing, and teacher-generated content, while more knowledgeable learners benefit more from independent problems, self-explanation, interleaving, longer spacing, and learner-generated content.
condition: When instructional support and practice format can be matched to learners' current expertise.
exception: Do not assume the same support is optimal at every stage of knowledge development.

statement: Applying learning science to educational practice is not a direct recipe because real settings contain interacting and partly hidden complexities.
condition: when translating research findings into practice or policy

statement: Practitioners should critically compare learning findings with evidence and policies in their own context, then adapt the findings beyond the narrow settings in which they were studied.
condition: when using learning research to guide educational strategy, policy, or research questions

statement: A learner's knowledge and cognitive resources develop through interacting cultural, social, cognitive, biological, developmental, and historical influences, so learner diversity is central rather than peripheral to explaining learning.
Different situations, contexts, and instructional strategies support different kinds of learning rather than producing a uniform learning process.
Learners continually combine deliberate and unconscious forms of learning, and this coordination is both shaped by their environment and consequential for later learning.
The brain remains adaptable across the life span, with learning reshaping neural connections while brain development and health in turn influence learning.
Successful learning requires coordination of multiple cognitive processes and the capacity to monitor and regulate one's own learning.
Learners' ability to monitor and regulate learning changes with age and can be strengthened through intervention.
Memory reconstructs prior experience rather than retrieving an exact stored copy.
Environmental cues strongly affect what a learner recalls and how newly encountered information becomes integrated with knowledge.
condition: when retrieving prior learning or connecting new information to it

statement: Prior knowledge can reduce the attention required for familiar activities and support new learning, but it can also bias attention toward existing schemas and away from new information.
exception: Its benefits do not eliminate schema-driven bias when a new problem differs from familiar ones.

statement: Overcoming biases induced by prior knowledge requires deliberate attention to information that does not fit an existing schema.
condition: when prior knowledge may be narrowing attention or driving an inappropriate familiar solution

statement: Learners extend knowledge by making logical connections that support generalization, categorization, inference, and novel problem solving.
Evidence-supported learning strategies include retrieval, learner-generated summaries and explanations, spaced presentation, and deliberate structuring of material.
Instruction should prompt learners to elaborate beyond presented material and apply it in varied contexts so they build organized, distinctive, and flexible knowledge structures.
condition: when the goal is durable understanding and transfer rather than short-term exposure

statement: The effectiveness of a learning strategy depends on the learner's existing skills and knowledge, the material, and the learning objective.
Educators should choose a learning strategy by matching its mechanism to the particular learner, setting, material, and objective rather than treating the strategy as universally effective.
condition: when selecting or adapting an instructional strategy

statement: Intentional learning requires sustained effort, perceived value, and a willingness to pursue the requested goal.
condition: for conscious, effortful learning

statement: Motivation is fostered when learners experience belonging and perceive agency and purpose in the learning environment.
Educators should support motivation by helping learners set valued learning goals and performance goals that are appropriately challenging.
condition: when designing support for engagement, persistence, and performance

statement: Learning experiences should support autonomy and control while helping learners recognize, monitor, and plan around their progress so that competence becomes visible and actionable.
condition: when seeking to sustain learner motivation

statement: Learning environments should be emotionally supportive and nonthreatening so learners feel safe and valued.
condition: when designing for motivation and sustained engagement

statement: Effective instruction depends on the interplay among learners' prior knowledge, experience, motivation, interests, language and cognitive skills; educators' own cultural experience; and the social, cognitive, cultural, and emotional learning environment.
Instruction should engage learners in directing their own learning through targeted feedback, metacognitive support, capacity-matched challenges, and meaningful goals.
condition: when fostering learner agency and self-regulation

statement: Education should use an asset model that helps learners connect academic goals with knowledge and learning opportunities from outside school.
condition: when designing curricula and instruction for diverse learners

statement: Deep understanding in an academic subject requires explicit teaching of that discipline's characteristic language and practices.
condition: when instruction aims for disciplinary understanding in fields such as science, history, or mathematics

statement: Assessment grounded in a well-defined model of learning can reveal the gap between a learner's current and desired performance and guide efforts to narrow it.
condition: when assessment is used to advance as well as monitor learning

statement: No learning technology is universally optimal; its effectiveness varies with learner characteristics, the target learning, sociocultural context, and the support available from instructors.
exception: Evidence of general effectiveness does not establish effectiveness for every learner or setting.

statement: A learning technology should be selected only when supporting evidence comes from situations sufficiently similar in learning goals, learner characteristics, environment, sociocultural context, and implementation support.
condition: when deciding whether to adopt a technology for learning

statement: Technology implementation should align with learning goals, include development and support for instructors and learners, and provide equitable access.
condition: when deploying technology in formal education or training

statement: Technology-supported learning should be monitored through ongoing assessment of learning and evaluation of implementation, with findings used to make improvements.
condition: after adopting a technology for education or training

statement: Across the life span, how much and how well people learn and transfer learning is influenced by their choices, motivation, self-regulation, capacity, opportunities, and circumstances.
Complex work, social engagement, physical activity, and adequate sleep are associated with continued learning and healthier aging.
condition: across adulthood and later life

statement: Learning should be treated as active adaptation through engagement with situations, problems, people, and ideas rather than as passive receipt of information.
condition: when designing or interpreting a learning experience

statement: Expertise reflects extensive, organized knowledge that changes what a person notices and how information is represented and interpreted, not merely stronger general memory, intelligence, or strategy use.
Deeper learning requires extending knowledge and skills beyond the narrow context in which they were first acquired.
condition: when the objective is adaptable knowledge rather than performance only in the original setting

statement: Instruction should help learners understand the conditions under which knowledge is useful, not only the knowledge itself.
condition: when preparing learners to select and apply knowledge independently

statement: Transfer to a new context is more likely when a learner understands the general principles beneath the original problem.
condition: when applying prior learning to a different problem or setting

statement: Constructing conceptual understanding of abstract ideas supports learning more effectively than accumulating disconnected information.
Learners are more successful and more able to sustain learning when they monitor themselves as learners and thinkers.
Children's learning and development emerge from interactions among their early competencies, environmental support and experience, and relationships with caregivers.
condition: during childhood development

statement: Learning changes the brain's physical organization, while changes in brain structure reorganize subsequent brain function and create different developmental periods of readiness.
condition: across development

statement: Culture influences every learner and learning purpose across settings, rather than operating only as a source of variation for selected groups or school situations.
Learning should be analyzed as a dynamic ecosystem spanning biological and physical conditions, individual cognition and affect, relationships, institutions, neighborhoods, society, and culture.
condition: when explaining learning outcomes or designing support

statement: A complete account of learning requires analysis across interdependent biological, cognitive, affective, interpersonal, and sociocultural levels.
condition: when synthesizing evidence about how learning develops over time

statement: Formal schooling occupies only a limited part of people's lives, while consequential knowledge and competencies also develop in families, communities, workplaces, and other informal settings.

Assessment of a learning study should give greatest weight to controlled evidence that includes participants varying on relevant characteristics, draws on multiple disciplines, and measures multiple learning outcomes.
condition: when such studies are available and relevant to the question
exception: Important questions may lack studies meeting all three criteria.

statement: Evidence synthesis in learning research should use methodological pluralism when ideal controlled studies are unavailable, while keeping the different inferential strengths of case, correlational, quasi-experimental, randomized, design, and practice studies visible.
condition: when the evidence base for an important topic contains heterogeneous designs

statement: Findings from different disciplines and settings cannot automatically be blended because their designs, samples, measures, and analytical methods may not be comparable.
condition: when integrating a heterogeneous learning-science evidence base

statement: Replicated findings, meta-analyses, and research syntheses warrant greater credence than an empirical result confined to a single study.
condition: when judging the strength of otherwise relevant learning evidence

statement: Findings based only on Western, educated, industrialized, affluent, democratic populations should not be generalized to all humans because those samples are not representative.
condition: when sample characteristics could influence the phenomenon under study
exception: Sample composition may be less consequential for some questions about broadly shared neurobiological structures.

statement: Laboratory findings about fundamental learning processes require substantial translation and interpretation before they can guide classroom practice.
condition: when the laboratory design or methodology cannot be reproduced practically in a classroom

statement: Useful expert knowledge is conditionalized: experts know when it applies and how to use it in context.
